operations.name: Arnold Lockshin

expected.name: Arnold Lockshin
expected.description: Arnold Lockshin was a Houston cancer researcher and Communist activist who moved with his wife and three children to Moscow in October 1986 after receiving Soviet political asylum. Lockshin said that the FBI had harassed his family and that his dismissal from a research laboratory was political retaliation for his Communist organizing and opposition to U.S. defense and foreign policy. His former employer said the dismissal concerned his research performance, and contemporary U.S. reporting did not substantiate all of his allegations. Lockshin remained in Russia and received Russian citizenship in 1992. This record attributes his persecution account to him rather than treating the disputed claim as a judicial finding.

operations.name: Karl Meyer

expected.name: Karl Meyer
expected.description:
Karl H. Meyer is a pacifist and long-running direct-action organizer associated with the Catholic Worker Movement and with war-tax resistance campaigns. His activism has emphasized nonviolent protest, voluntary poverty and mutual aid, and highly visible “public witness” actions meant to force attention to war, capital punishment, and government policy. He has also been involved in experimental protest tactics tied to tax resistance and public demonstrations.

Meyer’s arrests are a consistent feature of his activism rather than an exception. He participated in the 1961 peace march to Moscow and later staged long-distance protests (including a death-penalty protest walk dragging a mock electric chair). He has described decades of repeated arrests during protests and civil-disobedience actions, alongside sustained conflict with the Internal Revenue Service over tax-resistance tactics. In recent years he has remained active in Nashville, including an arrest in 2024 after intentionally sleeping on the Tennessee state-capitol grounds as a protest against a law escalating penalties for public camping. Son of former U.S. Representative William H. Meyer of Vermont, born in a cabin in northern Wisconsin. At age 19 he attempted to open a Catholic Worker house of hospitality in Washington, D.C.; on July 12, 1957 he met Dorothy Day and Ammon Hennacy at the Chrystie Street Catholic Worker. After witnessing the imprisonment of war tax resister Eroseanna Robinson, he vowed never to pay federal income tax again, pioneering the W-4 extra-allowances method to block withholding. He served two years in federal prison for tax resistance and shorter terms in 20 different jails. In 1984 he defied the IRS "frivolous filing" penalty by filing a frivolous return every day that year, was assessed $140,000 in penalties, and coined the term "cabbage patch resistance."

operations.name: Marie Equi

expected.name: Marie Equi
expected.description: Marie Equi was a physician and outspoken radical who linked her medical work to activism for labor rights, women’s equality, and anti-militarism, becoming a prominent figure in West Coast protest politics. Her opposition to World War I led to arrest and conviction under wartime sedition provisions; although she initially faced a longer term, her punishment was commuted to “a year and a day” by Woodrow Wilson. She began serving her sentence at San Quentin in October 1920 and was released in August 1921, after which her case remained a touchstone in debates over the criminalization of dissent
expected.body:
1920s custody review: Biographer Michael Helquist dates the start of Equi's San Quentin term to October 19, 1920. The Oregon Women's History Consortium account dates release for good behavior to August 9, 1921, also corroborated by Heather Mayer, Beyond the Rebel Girl, page 155. These improve the existing month-only endpoints. October 15 surrender in Portland and an October 17 departure report are distinct from October 19 prison admission. The sentence is clarified as three years commuted to one year and a day. Existing photograph and arrest date retained; conflicting online inmate numbers are not adopted without a register.

Source; Source; Source

1920s duration reconciliation: The source-supported interval 1920-10-19 through 1921-08-09 computes to 294 elapsed days (end minus start). This is the specific documented custody episode, not necessarily lifetime custody; earlier or later unquantified detention is excluded. Biographer Helquist dates October19,1920 SanQuentin admission; OregonWomensHistory and Mayer document August9,1921 release.294days prison interval supported. The previously blank audit expectation was superseded by this explicit evidence-based calculation; no event dates are changed here.

operations.name: A. J. Muste

expected.name: A. J. Muste
expected.description:
A. J. Muste was a clergyman who moved into labour and peace organising, becoming a central advocate of nonviolent direct action and a bridge between labour militancy and pacifist politics. He led Brookwood Labor College, and worked through the Fellowship of Reconciliation, the War Resisters League, Peacemakers and the Committee for Nonviolent Action. He died in New York City on February 11, 1967, aged 82. (Abraham Johannes Muste, born at Zierikzee in the Netherlands on January 8, 1885)

He was arrested repeatedly across nearly fifty years, and the pattern matters more than any single term: several separate political arrests and short detentions rather than one long sentence.

In February 1919, as spokesman for the striking textile workers at Lawrence, Massachusetts, he was beaten by police and pulled from a picket line, then charged with disturbing the peace and loitering. He was held about a week before eyewitness testimony supported his account and the charges were dismissed. In early September 1931 he was arrested at the Paterson silk strike alongside Norman Thomas and other labour supporters.

On June 15, 1955 he was one of twenty-nine pacifists who refused to take shelter during New York City's compulsory civil-defence drill and stayed above ground in City Hall Park. He was arraigned some nine hours later, bail was set at $1,500 a head, and the group was released within forty-eight hours after supporters raised more than $35,000. They were convicted on December 22, 1955 and their sentences suspended.

His best-documented jail term began on July 1, 1959, when he and other members of Omaha Action crossed the fence at a missile construction site near Mead, Nebraska. He refused bail and stayed in jail until his court appearance on July 9 — eight nights. The judge imposed six months and a $500 fine, then suspended both and placed him on a year's probation conditioned on his staying away from military-base demonstrations. He did not serve six months: later summaries sometimes confuse his suspended sentence with the imprisonment of other Omaha Action defendants.

On April 21, 1966, at eighty-one, he and five other American pacifists tried to demonstrate against the Vietnam War near the United States Embassy in Saigon. South Vietnamese police arrested them, held them in a detention room at the airport and expelled them from the country.

operations.name: Ricardo Flores Magón

expected.name: Ricardo Flores Magón
expected.description: Ricardo Flores Magón was a Mexican anarchist journalist and revolutionary organizer whose writing and organizing helped inspire the Mexican Revolution and shaped cross-border radical networks. Through the Partido Liberal Mexicano and allied publications, he promoted anti-authoritarian politics, labor militancy, and resistance to dictatorship, drawing repeated arrests in both Mexico and the United States. U.S. authorities prosecuted him multiple times, including a major World War I–era case in which he was arrested in 1918, convicted under the Espionage Act for antiwar writings, and sentenced to 20 years in federal prison. He died in custody in 1922 at Leavenworth, leaving a legacy defined by revolutionary agitation and the high costs of dissent.

operations.name: Mollie Steimer

expected.name: Mollie Steimer
expected.description:
Mollie Steimer was an anarchist activist in New York City whose organizing centered on opposition to war, state repression, and the criminalization of radical speech. In August 1918 she distributed leaflets condemning U.S. intervention against revolutionary Russia and calling on workers to resist militarism; she was arrested and later convicted under wartime sedition laws, receiving a 15-year prison sentence and a fine. After further arrests and a prolonged legal battle culminating in Abrams v. United States, her sentence was ultimately commuted on the condition of deportation, and she was expelled from the country in 1921. She continued political activity abroad, including advocacy for anarchist prisoners, reflecting a life shaped by both activism and forced exile.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Born 1897, Dunaivtsi, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Jewish. Garment worker. Migrated to US 1912, with parents and four siblings. Began working immediately after arrival, at age 16. Became an anarchist after discovering the writings of Peter Kropotkin; 1917 became a member of New York’s militant Jewish anarchist Shturem Group, which in 1918 became the Frayhayt Group. Arrested, with Hyman Lachowsky, while distributing radical leaflets protesting US intervention in the Russian Civil War on August 23, 1918. While out on bail, arrested eleven more times over eight months, including during a raid on the Union of Russian Workers’ People’s House in New York during the first Palmer Raids in November 1919. Convicted, with other members of the Frayhayt Group, for violation of the Espionage Act, and sentenced to 15 years in prison; after losing landmark Supreme Court free-speech case Abrams v. United States, sentence commuted on the condition of deportation. While detained on Ellis Island awaiting deportation, led a hunger strike to protest her segregation from other detainees. According to a supervisor, “Certainly it would not be safe to put her in a room with other detained females, this by reason of her known activities in spreading the propaganda of anarchism among among women and girls. Most of those detained female aliens will probably be admitted to the United States in due course, and to permit Mollie Steimer to sow the seeds of anarchism among them while they are the wards of the Government would be highly improper.” Deported November 1, 1921. 

In Russia, almost immediately involved in aid work for imprisoned anarchists; through this work she met her companion Senya Fleshin, an anarchist who had voluntarily returned from the US in 1917, and together they founded the Society to Help Anarchist Prisoners (with financial aid from comrades in the US). November 1922 both were arrested for this work and sentenced to two years internal exile in Siberia, but released after launching a hunger strike. Both arrested again July 9, 1923, for propagating anarchist ideas. Launched an eight-day hunger strike along with other political prisoners, including several other deportees from the US; Steimer and Fleshin given visas to Germany with the understanding that they would be executed if they returned to Russia, and left September 27, 1923. In Berlin, then after 1924 in Paris, the pair worked with Emma Goldman, Alexander Berkman, and other exiled Russian anarchists to aid radicals imprisoned in Russia. Steimer corresponded with, and was regularly visited by, anarchists from the US and elsewhere. In 1939 Steimer organized aid for refugees from the Spanish Civil War who had been placed in French internment camps; in May 1940, with the Nazi occupation of Paris, Steimer was herself sent to the internment camp in Gurs for seven weeks. After her release, she and Fleshin fled to Mexico, where they were aided by fellow deportees Jacob and Mary Abrams. Active in radical and exile circles in Mexico City, where they befriended Diego Rivera and Spanish anarchist exiles, and Fleshin ran a photography studio. Remained in constant correspondence with anarchists abroad. Steimer died of heart attack July 23, 1980 in Cuernavaca.

INS file 54517/73

See also: Senya Fléchine Papers and Emma Goldman Papers, International Institute of Social History, Amsterdam; Rose Pesotta Papers, New York Public Library; International Committee for Political Prisoners, Letters from Russian Prisons; Mollie Steimer: Toda una vida de lucha; Abe Bluestein, ed., Fighters for Anarchism: Mollie Steimer and Senya Fleshin; Paul Avrich, Anarchist Portraits; Richard Polenberg, Fighting Faiths: The Abrams Case, the Supreme Court, and Free Speech

operations.name: Jerome Zawada

expected.name: Jerome Zawada
expected.description:
Father Jerome 'Jerry' Zawada OFM was a Franciscan friar of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary Province (later the Sacred Heart Province) and a peace activist whose six decades of ministry included extensive work in the Philippines, in Nicaragua during the Contra war, and at U.S. military installations. He was arrested dozens of times across his life, primarily for SOA Watch line-crossings at Fort Benning, Georgia, and for protests at the Nevada Test Site, serving multiple short federal sentences. He died in 2017 at age 80.

Convicted in U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) for participating in the School of the Americas Watch (SOA Watch) annual nonviolent civil-disobedience action at Fort Benning, Georgia on September 2002. The action targeted the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC) — formerly the School of the Americas — which had trained Latin American military officers later linked to assassinations, torture, and massacres including Romero, the four U.S. churchwomen, the Jesuits in El Salvador, El Mozote, and Plan Cóndor. Defendants typically received 3 to 6 months in federal custody plus a fine.

operations.name: David Corcoran

expected.name: David Corcoran
expected.description:
David Corcoran crossed the line at Fort Benning, Georgia during the November 2000 SOA Watch vigil. Sentenced to 6 months, $1000 fine.

Each year on the November anniversary of the assassination of six Jesuits, their housekeeper, and her daughter at the University of Central America in San Salvador in 1989, peace activists gather at the gates of Fort Benning, Georgia, site of the U.S. Army School of the Americas / Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC), to commemorate the dead and to call for the school's closure. Hundreds have crossed the line onto the base over four decades of vigils; many have served federal sentences ranging from 30 days to a year for trespass.

The action targeted the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC) — formerly the School of the Americas — which had trained Latin American military officers later linked to assassinations, torture, and massacres. Defendants typically received 3 to 6 months in federal custody.

operations.name: Per Herngren

expected.name: Per Herngren
expected.description: Per Herngren is a Swedish peace activist and writer on nonviolence. On Easter morning, April 22, 1984, he was one of eight Pershing Plowshares activists who entered a Martin Marietta plant in Orlando, Florida, and hammered and poured blood on Pershing II and Patriot missile components. He received an eight-year U.S. sentence — longer than his co-defendants — and served about fifteen months across eleven prisons before being deported to Sweden.
expected.body:
Pershing Plowshares: custody episodes distinguished

The original May 1984 newsletter dates the action and initial detention to April 22, 1984 and reports continued detention while the eight refused bond. The August issue establishes sentencing on July 26, 1984. However, Jim Perkins subsequently described a period of freedom before the trial ended. The initial detention and later sentenced imprisonment are therefore recorded separately; the exact intervening release and later remand dates remain unresolved. The July 26 sentencing date is not silently treated as a new prison-admission date, and no arrest-to-final-release continuous total is inferred.

The sentence was three years for depredation and five years probation for conspiracy, with restitution. Christin Schmidt expressly corrected the earlier newsletter account of an extra suspended five-year term, and Perkins independently describes the same sentence.

Sources: Nuclear Resister 25, May 9, 1984, pages 1 and 3; issue 26, August 2, 1984, page 1; issue 27, December 3, 1984, page 10, Schmidt correction; Buddhist Peace Fellowship, Spring 1986, Perkins firsthand account pages 4-5.

Completion of the prison sentence on August 20, 1985 did not end confinement: immigration detention followed. The September newsletter reports an August 26 deportation flight, while his own September 7 letter describes a Tuesday evening departure, consistent with August 27 in that week. The departure is therefore recorded at August month precision with August 26-27 bounds rather than an unsupported exact-day choice. The stored August 1 is only a precision placeholder. Sources: Nuclear Resister 33-34, September 6, 1985, page 13; issue 36, December 9, 1985, page 6, firsthand letter.

operations.name: Charles Liteky

expected.name: Charles Liteky
expected.description:
Charles Liteky was a Roman Catholic Army chaplain in Vietnam, awarded the Medal of Honor for carrying 20+ wounded soldiers through fire to evacuation on December 6, 1967 near Phuoc Lac. Left the priesthood 1975; married former nun Judy Balch 1983. On July 29, 1986 became the first and only Medal of Honor recipient to renounce his medal, placing it in an envelope addressed to President Reagan near the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. With George Mizo, began the Veterans Fast for Life on the U.S. Capitol steps September 1, 1986 — a 47-day water-only fast against Contra aid. Repeatedly arrested at the School of the Americas; in June 2000 sentenced to 1 year at Lompoc (with 70 days solitary) plus $10,000 fine for trespassing at Fort Benning. Charles Liteky was an United States Army chaplain who served in Vietnam and received the Medal of Honor for battlefield heroism. After leaving the priesthood, he became a nationally visible peace activist who argued that his wartime experience imposed a moral duty to oppose U.S. militarism, especially in Central America and in U.S.-backed security training linked to repression.

In 1986 he renounced his Medal of Honor by leaving it at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial as a political act. He became a leading figure in protests against the School of the Americas at Fort Benning, repeatedly accepting arrest for nonviolent civil disobedience and trespass during demonstrations. Courts imposed prison sentences and significant fines for those actions, including a one-year sentence in 2000 for repeated base trespass. He spent his later years in San Francisco, continuing public opposition to war and state violence.

operations.name: George Mizo

expected.name: George Mizo
expected.description: George Mizo was a decorated Army combat infantry sergeant in Vietnam who served at Khe Sanh, wounded in a firefight and evacuated just before NVA troops overran the base in the Tet Offensive and wiped out his unit. Operated in areas heavily sprayed with Agent Orange. Joined Vietnam Veterans Against the War, returned his medals to the Pentagon. With Charles Liteky, began the Veterans Fast for Life on the U.S. Capitol steps September 1, 1986. Married German peace activist Rosemarie Höhn-Mizo (met 1986); they founded the Vietnam Friendship Village near Hanoi in 1992 caring for Agent Orange victims. Died March 18, 2002 of complications from his own Agent Orange exposure.
expected.body:
Capitol fast is not a custody interval

Bill Davis's original account in The Veteran (Winter 1987), published by Vietnam Veterans Against the War, identifies Mizo and Charles Liteky as beginning their voluntary Capitol-steps fast on September 1, 1986. It describes daily vigils, public appearances and supporters, and announces a second phase on October 17. The previously entered August 31 arrest and prison-admission dates have no support in that account and contradicted this entry's existing statement that he was not arrested at the fast. They are removed, not replaced by the date the protest began. Ending the fast is not a release from prison; its reported 47 days are not days incarcerated.

Sources: Bill Davis, VVAW National Office, Putting Their Lives On The Line!, The Veteran, Winter 1987, page 17; Peace House, reproducing participant S. Brian Willson's own account and caption of the 1986 fast. Existing identified photograph retained. This correction concerns the 1986 protest only; it makes no claim about Mizo's separate earlier military imprisonment.

expected.description: World War II conscientious objector who served with an Allied ambulance unit through North Africa, Italy, France, and Germany; was with British troops liberating Bergen-Belsen. operations.name: Marvin Allen Davidov

expected.name: Marvin Allen Davidov
expected.description: Marvin Allen Davidov was born in Detroit on August 26, 1931, moved to St. Paul in 1949 to attend Macalester College and served in the U.S. Army 1953-1955. A 1961 Freedom Rider arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, and a participant in the 1963-1964 Canada-to-Cuba Peace Walk, he founded the Honeywell Project in 1968 after reading a Staughton Lynd article calling on activists to target war-profiteering corporations. He led the Project for over two decades, organizing annual protests at Honeywell's Minneapolis headquarters and shareholder meetings against cluster bombs, missile-guidance systems, anti-personnel mines, and depleted-uranium munitions. Co-authored "You Can't Do That" (2010) with Carol Masters.
expected.body:
Custody-date source review

North Star Legal Foundation v. Honeywell Project, 355 N.W.2d 186 (1984), describes mass trespass arrests on April 18 and October 24, 1983. Davidov is named as a civil respondent, but the opinion does not supply his individual criminal arrest, admission, or release dates. The unsupported October 23 dates are therefore removed rather than replaced with the mass-action date.

St. Louis Park Historical Society's history, based in part on material and an interview provided by Davidov, reports his repeated arrests and three jail sentences across the campaign. Its combined jail total belongs to the group, not Davidov individually. The December 12, 1986 Nuclear Resister, printed page 6, separately reports a recent Davidov conviction with a one-day community-service sentence; that is not evidence of a prison day or of the 1983 case's outcome. Individual custody endpoints remain unknown. His existing identified portrait is retained.

expected.description: Polly H. Mann was born in Lonoke, Arkansas, and co-founded Women Against Military Madness (WAMM) with Marianne Hamilton at Loretta's Tea Room in Minneapolis in fall 1981, alongside eight other women. WAMM became a frequent partner of the Honeywell Project and Mann was repeatedly arrested at Honeywell shareholder-meeting actions through the 1980s. Ran for U.S. Senate as an independent in 1988 with the motto "Speak Truth to Power," and remained active into her 100s. Died at age 103.
expected.body:
Individual custody dates remain unresolved

North Star Legal Foundation v. Honeywell Project, 355 N.W.2d 186, is a civil taxpayer lawsuit, not Mann's individual criminal prosecution. It describes mass arrests on April 18 and October 24, 1983, but supplies no individual custodial endpoints for Mann. The unsupported October 23 arrest and admission dates are therefore removed. Mann's own February 5, 1996 MPR interview confirms a five-day jail stay, apparently in the Ramsey County workhouse, but does not date it or link it to this case. No date or served-day counter is inferred from that recollection. Existing identified portrait retained.

operations.name: Erica Bouza

expected.name: Erica Bouza
expected.description: Erica Bouza was the wife of then-Minneapolis Police Chief Tony Bouza. Became national news in April 1983 when she and 138 other anti-nuclear protesters sat down in front of Honeywell's Minneapolis headquarters and were arrested by officers under her husband's command. Arrested again on October 24, 1983 in the second mass sit-in (577 arrests) and sentenced to 10 days at the Hennepin County workhouse. Featured in People Magazine. The first of approximately 11 peace-related civil-disobedience arrests in the Twin Cities.
expected.body:
Photograph provenance and separate custody events

The original 900 by 900 photograph is captioned Erica and Tony Bouza at the Wellfleet OysterFest, courtesy Richard Rosenthal, in the Provincetown Independent's named family obituary. Both subjects are retained; it is a later life photograph, not a 1983 arrest image. Photograph date and reuse license remain unknown; no new crop or reconstruction is used.

The October blockade date is October 24, not October 23, corroborated by local historical chronology and Winona LaDuke's movement account. The original November 11, 1983 Evening Herald carries UPI reporting that Bouza was then serving her ten-day workhouse sentence. A November 1 placeholder is not an exact release and must not produce a nine-day served total. Unsupported custody endpoints and that total are cleared. Her April 18 arrest and citation-release were a separate event; they do not establish admission for the later workhouse sentence.

operations.name: Eugene Debs

expected.name: Eugene Debs
expected.description: Eugene Debs was the foremost American socialist of his era — locomotive fireman, founder of the American Railway Union (1893), leader of the 1894 Pullman Strike, IWW co-founder (1905), five-time Socialist presidential candidate. On June 16, 1918 he delivered an anti-war speech in Canton, Ohio condemning U.S. involvement in WWI; convicted under the Espionage Act on Sept 12, 1918 and sentenced to 10 years. Served at Moundsville (WV) and Atlanta Federal Penitentiary, where in 1920 he received nearly 920, 000 votes for president as "Convict No. 9653." Harding commuted his sentence to time served on Dec 23, 1921; he walked out of Atlanta on Christmas Day. Died Oct 20, 1926 of cardiovascular disease aggravated by imprisonment. Eugene Victor Debs was the most prominent socialist in U.S. history — five-time Socialist Party of America presidential candidate, founder of the American Railway Union (which led the 1894 Pullman Strike, for which Debs served six months at the Woodstock IL jail), and co-founder of the Industrial Workers of the World in 1905. On June 16, 1918, in Canton, Ohio, Debs delivered a public speech denouncing U.S. participation in World War I and the prosecution of socialist anti-war organizers. He was arrested two weeks later under the Espionage Act of 1917, convicted September 12, 1918 in federal court in Cleveland, and sentenced to ten years in federal prison. He began serving in April 1919 at the West Virginia State Penitentiary in Moundsville, then was transferred to the United States Penitentiary in Atlanta. From his cell as Federal Prisoner #9653, Debs ran for president of the United States in 1920 on the Socialist Party ticket and received 919, 799 votes — nearly one million Americans voting for a presidential candidate then in federal prison. President Warren G. Harding commuted Debs's sentence to time served on Christmas Day 1921; Debs was released December 25, 1921 after serving roughly two and a half years. Eugene Debs was a leading figure in the American labor movement

operations.name: Charles Emil Ruthenberg

expected.name: Charles Emil Ruthenberg
expected.description:
Charles Emil Ruthenberg was born to Prussian Lutheran immigrants in Cleveland; joined the SP in 1909 and edited the Cleveland Socialist. After the U.S. entered WWI he organized antiwar rallies; on May 17, 1917 he gave a Cleveland speech for which he, Alfred Wagenknecht, and Charles Baker were arrested for obstructing the draft — the first such Espionage Act convictions in the United States. Sentenced to one year, served roughly 10 months at the Stark County Workhouse in Canton, Ohio. Re-arrested repeatedly through the 1920s; founded the Communist Party USA in Chicago in September 1919 and became its first National Secretary. Died March 1, 1927; ashes interred in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis.

Ruthenberg was imprisoned twice more after the draft case. Convicted under New York's Criminal Anarchy Act, he was sentenced on October 29, 1920 and held at Clinton Prison at Dannemora until he was released on bond on April 24, 1922; that conviction was afterwards reversed. He was among those arrested in the raid on the underground Communist Party convention at Bridgman, Michigan on August 22, 1922, and a jury convicted him under Michigan's Criminal Syndicalism Act on May 12, 1923. The Michigan Supreme Court affirmed in January 1925, but he remained at liberty through the appeals and never served that sentence; he died on March 1, 1927.

operations.name: Victor Berger

expected.name: Victor Berger
expected.description: Victor Berger was born in Nieder-Rehbach, Austria-Hungary; emigrated 1878. Edited the Milwaukee Leader (1911–29) and built the "Sewer Socialist" machine that made him in 1910 the first Socialist elected to the U.S. House. Indicted Feb 2, 1918 in the Chicago "Trial of Five" before Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis; convicted Jan 8, 1919 and sentenced to 20 years. The House twice refused to seat him (1919, 1920). SCOTUS reversed in Berger v. United States, 255 U.S. 22 (1921), holding Landis should have recused. Re-elected 1922; served three more terms (1923–29). Died Aug 7, 1929 of streetcar-accident injuries. Victor Berger was the first Socialist elected to the United States Congress, representing Milwaukee, Wisconsin. He was indicted in February 1918 under the Espionage Act of 1917 for editorials he had published in the Milwaukee Leader opposing U.S. entry into World War I. He was convicted on January 8, 1919 in U.S. District Court in Chicago and sentenced on February 20, 1919 by Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis to twenty years in federal prison. Berger had been re-elected to Congress in November 1918 while under indictment; the House refused to seat him on November 10, 1919 and again, after a Wisconsin special election returned him in December 1919. On January 31, 1921, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed Berger's conviction in Berger v. United States, holding that Judge Landis's hostility toward Berger's German-American ancestry deprived him of an impartial trial. The federal indictment was dismissed in 1922 and Berger was finally seated in the House in 1923, serving three more terms.

operations.name: Charles Ashleigh

expected.name: Charles Ashleigh
expected.description:
Charles Ashleigh was an English-born IWW poet, journalist, and orator who delivered the eulogy at the 1916 funeral of the Everett Massacre martyrs and authored the poem "Everett, November Fifth." Convicted in the 1918 Chicago IWW trial; sentenced to 10 years at Leavenworth. Released in the December 1921 amnesty; deported to Britain in April 1922. Attended the Fourth Comintern Congress; remained a lifelong activist with the Communist Party of Great Britain.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Raised in a middle-class environment, Ashleigh joined the Independent Labour Party at age fifteen, later affiliating with the Fabian Society and the Social Democratic Federation. He served as a secretary of the Fabian Society from 1908 and was active in the socialist Clarion Scouts. At the behest of the ILP, he organized among South Wales coal miners in 1908–9. In 1909 he moved to Buenos Aires to work as a clerk with the Central Argentine Railroad, founded a Socialist Club there, and wrote for the Buenos Aires Herald. After traveling on foot through Argentina, Chile, and Peru, he worked his way as a crew member to Portland in 1912, then regularized his legal status by crossing between Canada and the United States. He became a paid speaker for the Socialist Party of America, but soon aligned himself with the IWW and became a paid organizer. He traveled extensively as a journalist, wrote poetry, and participated in the Rangel-Cline and Everett defense campaigns. Openly gay, he maintained a romantic relationship with African American radical poet Claude McKay. Arrested in 1917, he was a defendant in the federal IWW trial and received a ten-year sentence and a $30,000 fine. He joined the Communist Party while incarcerated, and his sentence was commuted in 1921 on the condition of his voluntary departure on February 7, 1922.

In London, Ashleigh transferred to the Communist Party of Great Britain and worked for the Sunday Worker, Daily Worker, and TASS. In 1922 he was dispatched to India to deliver invitations to the Fourth Comintern Congress but was detained and expelled by British authorities, yet was able to complete his mission. Later that year, he worked as a translator at the Fourth Comintern Congress in Moscow and was asked to establish an American information section for the Red International of Labor Unions, and moved to Berlin in 1923 to work for the RILU. He was arrested and expelled from Germany shortly thereafter. Published his semi-autobiographical IWW novel The Rambling Kid in 1930. Sent to Moscow in 1931 to write for The Moscow News/Moscow Daily News, he was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1934 after being denounced as homosexual by a roommate. He remained a member of the CPGB until his death in 1974, though largely marginalized within it.

operations.name: Jacob Abrams

expected.name: Jacob Abrams
expected.description:
Jacob Abrams was a Russian-Jewish anarchist bookbinder and lead defendant in the landmark First Amendment case Abrams v. United States, 250 U.S. 616 (1919). On August 22-23, 1918 he and four others were arrested in New York for throwing Yiddish and English leaflets from a Lower East Side rooftop denouncing Wilson's deployment of U.S. troops to Soviet Russia. Convicted Oct 23, 1918 under the Sedition Act; sentenced to 20 years and $1,000 fine. SCOTUS upheld 7-2 (famous Holmes/Brandeis "marketplace of ideas" dissent). Served roughly 3 years at Atlanta; deported to Soviet Russia aboard SS Estonia Nov 24, 1921; later left USSR for Mexico, where he died 1953. He was born January 24, 1886 — the 1883 given in some references is the weaker reading — and died in Mexico on June 10, 1953; a temporary medical readmission to the United States shortly before his death did not end the exile his conditional pardon imposed.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): A prominent Jewish anarchist in New York, he belonged to the group that published the underground Yiddish newspapers Shturem (1917) and Frayhayt (1918). Married fellow anarchist Mary Domsky, a survivor of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire. Arrested in 1918 for printing and distributing leaflets opposing US intervention in the Russian Civil War, he was the central defendant in the landmark Supreme Court case Abrams v. United States. Following their conviction, he and the other defendants were released to be deported to Soviet Russia on November 23, 1921.

In Russia founded at a steam laundry for Comintern employees and worked with the anarcho-syndicalist Golos Truda press and bookstore, but soon became disillusioned and left with Mary for Paris in 1925, then Mexico City in 1926. There he was active among exiled Spanish anarchists of the Tierra y Libertad group and associated with Leon Trotsky. Co-founded the Yiddish antifascist newspaper Di Shtime in Mexico City 1939. After a cancer diagnosis in 1945 he was temporarily readmitted to the US under FBI supervision for medical treatment, and he died 1953 in Mexico.

operations.name: Hyman Lachowsky

expected.name: Hyman Lachowsky
expected.description:
Hyman Lachowsky was a Russian-Jewish bookbinder and Frayhayt-group anarchist convicted alongside Jacob Abrams. Eyewitnesses testified he was severely beaten by police during interrogation. Convicted Oct 23, 1918 under the Sedition Act; sentenced to 20 years and $1,000 fine. Deported to Soviet Russia Nov 24, 1921 aboard SS Estonia. Returned to his hometown in present-day Belarus; reported to have perished under Nazi occupation during the Holocaust. Born in 1894, his death is unresolved: Kenyon Zimmer’s reconstruction from INS and FBI files puts it about 1961, while earlier accounts say he was probably murdered by the Nazis in Minsk after the German occupation began in 1941. Because the accounts conflict, no death date is recorded.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): In 1917 Lachowsky joined New York’s militant Jewish anarchist Shturem Group, which became the Frayhayt Group in 1918. On August 23, 1918, he was arrested with Molly Steimer while distributing leaflets protesting US intervention in the Russian Civil War. Beaten during interrogation, he was convicted with other group members under the Espionage Act and sentenced to twenty years in prison and a $1,000 fine. In October 1919 he declared to immigration agents, “I am an alien and an anarchist…I am opposed to all organized government. Not only the Government of the United States but any government…I’m an anarchist and proud of it.” By 1921, however, he had become disillusioned and renounced anarchism. After losing the Supreme Court free-speech case Abrams v. United States, he was deported November 23, 1921.

Disillusioned with radicalism, he returned to Minsk, started a family, and stayed out of politics. He reportedly died of natural causes sometime before the Second World War.

expected.description:
Samuel Lipman was 21 at the time of his arrest; the lone Marxist socialist (rather than anarchist) among the Abrams defendants and a worker in the fur trade. Deported to Soviet Russia Nov 24, 1921. There became a Communist Party member and economist; arrested in Stalin's Great Purge and reportedly executed in 1937.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Lipman belonged to the Socialist Party of America as well as New York’s anarchist Frayhayt Group, and identified as a leftwing socialist and Marxist rather than an anarchist. A pacifist and vegetarian strongly influenced by Leo Tolstoy, he lived with anarchist Ethel Bernstein, his common-law wife. In 1918 he was arrested with others for distributing leaflets opposing US intervention in the Russian Civil War and sentenced to twenty years under the Espionage Act. While imprisoned he became disillusioned with Tolstoy and falsely claimed anarchist beliefs in hopes of deportation. After losing the landmark Supreme Court free-speech case Abrams v. United States, he was deported November 23, 1921. 

In Russia he married Bernstein, studied agronomy, and became chairman of the Department of Economic Geography at the University of the Toilers of the East. In 1928 he applied to join the Communist Party. During Stalin’s purges in the 1930s he was executed.

operations.name: Luigi Galleani

expected.name: Luigi Galleani
expected.description:
Luigi Galleani was the leading insurrectionary anarchist theorist among Italian immigrants in early 20th-century America. From June 6, 1903 edited Cronaca Sovversiva ("Subversive Chronicle") in Barre, Vermont and later Lynn, Massachusetts. His followers, the Galleanisti, carried out the 1919 anarchist bombings and the Wall Street bombing of 1920; Sacco and Vanzetti were Galleanisti. Federal agents shut down Cronaca Sovversiva June 17, 1917. Deported to Italy June 24, 1919 along with eight followers (the "Galleani 9"). In Italy repeatedly imprisoned and exiled under Mussolini until his death 1931.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Became an anarchist while studying law at the University of Turin. After fleeing police repression in Italy, he lived in France and Switzerland, working with anarchist geographer Élisée Reclus, before being arrested, expelled, and imprisoned in Italy. While confined to the island of Pantelleria, he met his wife Maria. He escaped in 1900 and fled to Egypt and England before immigrating to the United States in 1901.

In the United States, edited La Questione Sociale in Paterson, New Jersey, and led the 1902 silk workers’ strike, for which he was indicted for inciting riot and fled to Canada, then Barre, Vermont, where founded newspaper Cronaca Sovversiva in 1903. Later relocated the paper to Lynn, Massachusetts. Emerged as the leading Italian anarchist proponent of insurrectionary violence. Deported on June 24, 1919, leaving his wife and six children behind.

Upon arrival in Italy, briefly arrested and then relaunched Cronaca Sovversiva in Turin. Imprisoned for sedition in 1922, and again arrested in 1926, serving prison time followed by internal exile. He remained under surveillance until his death in 1931.

expected.description: Evan Welling Thomas was the younger brother of Norman Thomas; Princeton seminary student studying in Edinburgh when the U.S. entered WWI; returned home and refused induction as an absolutist conscientious objector. After leading a hunger strike at Fort Riley, Kansas in August 1918, court-martialed, sentenced to life imprisonment, transferred to Fort Leavenworth, where held in solitary confinement and chained handcuffed to his cell door for 14 days. operations.name: Philip Grosser

expected.name: Philip Grosser
expected.description:
Philip Grosser was born in Slavuta, Ukraine 1890; established anarchist activist in Boston by 1917; among the first to refuse the draft on political — rather than religious — grounds. Court-martialed and sent to Alcatraz; refused the uniform, refused to stand in formation, and refused "hard labor"; retaliated against with extended solitary, beatings, being dragged on a rope, denial of toilet facilities, and confinement in Alcatraz's "iron maidens" (upright iron cages). After release wrote one of the earliest published exposés of conditions at Alcatraz, the 32-page pamphlet "Alcatraz – Uncle Sam's Devil's Island" (1933). Took his own life in Boston Oct 1933.

Philip B. Grosser was a conscientious objector from Massachusetts imprisoned during World War I. Court-martialed for refusing military service, he was held at Fort Leavenworth; Alcatraz Island. Sentenced to 30 years in prison on Aug. (Documented in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection's World War I Conscientious Objectors database.) Archival note: registered for draft on June 5, 1917, as a C.O.; arrested in Boston in Dec. 1917 for failing to report for military duty; interviewed by Bd. in Feb. ___ at Leavenworth; …
expected.body:
1920s remaining-entry review: Philip Grosser's firsthand account, Uncle Sam's Devil's Island (Kate Sharpley Library reprint), printed pages 6-9 and 17-18, distinguishes his initial 1917 civil arrest and $500 bond from military custody beginning in December 1917. He describes Fort Banks, Fort Andrews, arrival at Fort Jay on June 11, 1918, later Leavenworth confinement, and departure for Alcatraz in June 1919. These are stages of one military imprisonment, not two independent sentences or a release in December 1919. The first inherited record is retained as the earlier custody stage; its false release is removed, and its institution field is left unassigned because December 1917 was not Leavenworth admission. The Alcatraz record is retained as the later stage, with admission at year precision pending its admission register. The inherited August 14, 1917 arrest/admission and December 14, 1920 release are unsupported by this account. His memoir dates the release order December 2, 1920 but describes continued solitary confinement over unsigned discharge papers before freedom; December 1920 is therefore retained at month precision, not an invented exact departure day. Existing portrait retained. No case is deleted and transfers are not recorded as releases.

operations.name: Joseph Franklin Rutherford

expected.name: Joseph Franklin Rutherford
expected.description: Joseph Franklin Rutherford was a Missouri-born lawyer; successor to Charles Taze Russell as president of the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society. Lead defendant in the May 1918 federal indictment of eight Watch Tower directors known as the "Rutherford 8" — charged under the Espionage Act of 1917 with attempting to cause insubordination by distributing the millenarian book The Finished Mystery. After trial in EDNY (Brooklyn), jury convicted June 20, 1918; Judge Harland B. Howe imposed 20-year sentences June 21. Defendants entered the U.S. Penitentiary at Atlanta; served roughly nine months, released on bail March 1919 after Justice Brandeis granted relief. Convictions reversed on appeal 1919; charges dropped 1920. Renamed the movement "Jehovah's Witnesses" in 1931.

operations.name: Risley W. Young

expected.name: Risley W. Young
expected.description: Rosley W. Young was one of the thirteen soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment hanged at Camp Travis, near San Antonio, at dawn on 11 December 1917, after the first Houston-riot court-martial (the "Nesbit case"). The executions were carried out in secret, within a day of sentencing and without the War Department review that would normally have allowed an appeal. The Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny) erupted on 23 August 1917 after Houston police, enforcing Jim Crow, beat and arrested soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment. About 150 soldiers marched on the city; the night left some twenty people dead. In the largest court-martial in U.S. history, 118 men were tried, 19 executed, and 63 sentenced to life imprisonment. In 2023 the U.S. Army set aside all 110 convictions and honorably discharged the soldiers. (Recorded as Private Rosley W. Young)

operations.name: Thomas Mooney

expected.name: Thomas Mooney
expected.description: Thomas Mooney was a San Francisco labor organizer and IWW militant — son of an Irish coal-miner Knights of Labor organizer — who along with Warren K. Billings was framed for the July 22, 1916 Preparedness Day Parade bombing on Market Street that killed ten and injured forty. Convicted of first-degree murder in 1917 on perjured testimony; sentenced to death. President Wilson, alarmed that Mooney's execution might trigger Russian-style worker revolt, personally interceded with California Governor William Stephens, who in 1918 commuted the sentence to life. The case became a 22-year international cause célèbre. Pardoned by Governor Culbert L. Olson on January 7, 1939. Thomas Mooney was San Francisco labor leader and socialist activist. On July 22, 1916, a parade was organized in San Francisco by local supporters of the Preparedness Movement which advocated American entry into World War I. A suitcase bomb was detonated by an unknown assailant, killing 10. Mooney and labor leader Warren Billings were both framed for the bombing by the San Francisco Police Department using falsified evidence and perjured testimony from a paid off witness, Frank Oxman. On November 1920, Draper Hand of the SFPD went to Mayor James Rolph and admitted that he had helped Charles Fickert and Martin Swanson frame Mooney. Later, two witnesses, Edgar Rigall and Earl K. Hatcher, came forward and provided evidence that Frank Oxman was 200 miles away during the bombing and could not have seen what he told the court at the trial of Mooney. In February 1921, John McDonald confessed that the police had forced him to lie about the planting of the bomb. Despite this new evidence the Californian authorities refused a retrial. Mooney served 22 years in prison before finally being pardoned in 1939 by Governor Culbert Olson. By then, Mooney had been suffering from jaundice and ulcers from his time and prison and died shortly after in 1942 at age 59.

expected.name: Warren Billings
expected.description:
Warren Billings was born in Middletown, New York on Independence Day 1893; young shoe-workers' organizer convicted before Mooney to provide a "predicate" conspirator. Sentenced to life for second-degree murder in the 1916 San Francisco Preparedness Day bombing. Held at Folsom State Prison, where he learned watchmaking. After 23 years, 2 months and 20 days of imprisonment — the longest of any Wilson-era political prisoner in the United States — California Governor Culbert L. Olson commuted his sentence to time served in 1939. Full pardon from Governor Edmund G. "Pat" Brown in 1961. Warren BIllings was an anarchist and labor leader who was convicted for possession of dynamite. Warren claims he had no idea what was inside the suitcase and was ordered to bring it somewhere when he was arrested. Much of the prosecution's case depending on Warren's alleged ties to Thomas Mooney, a socialist and militant accused of a San Fransisco bombing killing ten people. It is alleged that at the trial witnessed were coached by the detective and the prosecutor. Both Warren and Thomas were found guilty and sentenced to death, but President Wilson stepped in and urged the governor to decrease their sentences to life in prison after immense public outcry. He was released in 1939 and finally pardoned in 1961.

Warren K. Billings was a young shoe-worker and union militant who, like Tom Mooney, was framed for the July 22, 1916 Preparedness Day Parade bombing in San Francisco. Convicted in September 1916 on the perjured testimony of witness Frank Oxman, he was sentenced to life imprisonment at Folsom State Prison, where he served 23 years. He was paroled in 1939 and finally received a full pardon from California Governor Earl Warren in 1961.

1920s remaining-entry review: The Pampa News, October 18, 1939, page 6, carries an Associated Press report datelined San Francisco that day. Billings had awakened in a room rather than a cell and met his fiancee the previous night after release. This confirms completed release October 17, not merely the earlier commutation order or a planned departure. The complete original page was visually checked; month precision is upgraded to day.

expected.name: Charlotte Anita Whitney
expected.description: Charlotte Anita Whitney was a Wellesley-educated heiress (great-niece of Supreme Court Justice Stephen J. Field), social worker, and California suffrage and NAACP organizer who became a charter member of the Communist Labor Party in 1919. Arrested November 28, 1919 after a speech to the Oakland Civic Club; charged with five counts under California's brand-new Criminal Syndicalism Act. Conviction unanimously upheld in Whitney v. California, 274 U.S. 357 (1927) — most famous for Justice Brandeis's concurring opinion articulating the "clear and present danger" standard. June 20, 1927 California Governor C.C. Young granted her an unconditional pardon.

January 1 and February 1 are storage anchors for year/month precision, not asserted event days. The prior San Quentin attribution and exact duration are removed; no penitentiary admission is established. The inconsistent November arrest day remains under review.

operations.name: Margaret Sanger

expected.name: Margaret Sanger
expected.description: Margaret Sanger was the founder of the first U.S. birth-control clinic at 46 Amboy Street, Brownsville, Brooklyn on October 16, 1916, with her sister Ethel Byrne and interpreter Fania Mindell. The clinic served some 400 women in 10 days before an undercover policewoman shut it down on October 26, 1916, arresting all three. Charged under New York's Comstock obscenity statute, tried in early 1917 before a three-judge panel and sentenced to 30 days in Queens County Penitentiary. The 1918 New York Court of Appeals "Crane decision" upheld her conviction but for the first time permitted physicians to prescribe contraceptives. Margaret Higgins Sanger was an American nurse, sex educator, and birth control activist who founded the first birth control clinic in the United States. On October 16, 1916, she opened the clinic in a storefront at 46 Amboy Street in the Brownsville neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York. Within ten days, undercover police arrested Sanger, her sister Ethel Byrne, and clinic worker Fania Mindell for distributing contraceptives and contraceptive information in violation of New Yorks Comstock-era anti-obscenity statutes. Sanger was tried in early 1917 and sentenced to 30 days in the Queens County Penitentiary, which she served. The arrests catalyzed national press coverage and a sustained legal campaign that gradually weakened state-level Comstock restrictions. Sanger went on to found what became the Planned Parenthood Federation of America. Her broader record included support for eugenics policies common in the Progressive Era — a serious and well-documented part of her history that the modern Planned Parenthood organization has formally repudiated.

expected.description: LeRoy Nathaniel Bundy was a dentist and the principal Black political organizer in East St. Louis, Illinois at the time of the July 2, 1917 race massacre. Convicted March 28, 1919 in Waterloo, Illinois on testimony from Edward Wilson who himself admitted Bundy had not participated; sentenced to life imprisonment. Moved to Cleveland, earned law degree at Western Reserve, became prominent UNIA leader.

operations.name: John Theodore Glick

expected.name: John Theodore Glick
expected.description: John Theodore “Ted” Glick, born in Huntingdon, Pennsylvania, is an American antiwar, progressive and climate-justice activist. After leaving Grinnell College in 1969 he publicly refused induction into the United States military and became active in the Catholic Left campaign of nonviolent resistance to the Vietnam War. On September 6, 1970 he and seven others entered the federal building in Rochester, New York and ransacked federal offices and government records, Selective Service material among them, intending to disrupt the draft. Representing himself at trial, he was convicted with all seven co-defendants on December 1, 1970 and sentenced on December 3 to concurrent terms of up to eighteen months. He served roughly eleven months in federal custody, at the federal youth institution at Ashland, Kentucky, at FCI Danbury in Connecticut and at the federal facility at Springfield, Missouri; at Danbury he joined a prison hunger strike in August 1971 and was put in solitary confinement. He was released on appeal bond on October 28, 1971. While he was still imprisoned he was added, on April 30, 1971, to the superseding indictment in the Harrisburg Eight case, which alleged a conspiracy to kidnap Henry Kissinger, damage federal heating tunnels, possess explosives and destroy government records; because he insisted on representing himself his case was severed from the others, and the government never brought the severed prosecution to trial. On June 29, 1972 the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed the Rochester conviction, holding that the trial judge had prejudicially communicated with the jury outside Glick’s presence during its deliberations. He has continued since as a progressive organizer, writer, antiwar activist and climate-justice campaigner.

expected.description: One of approximately 1,500 activists arrested between 1999 and 2003 for civil disobedience at the U.S. Navy's Atlantic Fleet Weapons Training Facility on the island of Vieques, Puerto Rico. The campaign — sparked by the April 19, 1999 death of civilian Navy security guard David Sanes Rodríguez when an errant Marine F/A-18 bomb struck his observation post — drew Puerto Ricans of every political stripe (independentistas, statehooders, the Catholic Church, fishers, environmentalists) into a sustained nonviolent direct-action campaign demanding the Navy leave Vieques. Defendants were prosecuted in U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) and typically served 30 to 90 days in federal custody, most often at MDC Guaynabo. The Navy formally ceased operations on Vieques on May 1, 2003. Listed as a current prisoner in Nuclear Resister Issue #121 "Inside & Out" prisoner roster.

The campaign — sparked by the April 19, 1999 death of civilian Navy security guard David Sanes Rodríguez when an errant Marine F/A-18 bomb struck his observation post — drew Puerto Ricans of every political stripe (independentistas, statehooders, the Catholic Church, fishers, environmentalists) into a sustained nonviolent direct-action campaign demanding the Navy leave Vieques. Defendants were prosecuted in U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) and typically served 30 to 90 days in federal custody, most often at MDC Guaynabo. The Navy formally ceased operations on Vieques on May 1, 2003. Listed as a current prisoner in Nuclear Resister Issue #121 "Inside & Out" prisoner roster.

Defendants were prosecuted in U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) and typically served 30 to 90 days in federal custody, most often at MDC Guaynabo. The Navy formally ceased operations on Vieques on May 1, 2003. Listed as a current prisoner in Nuclear Resister Issue #121 "Inside & Out" prisoner roster.

expected.name: Heriberto Marín
expected.description:
Heriberto Marín Torres (born November 23, 1928, in Barrio Coabey, Jayuya) was one of the youngest fighters of the 1950 Nationalist insurrection — a Nationalist cadet who helped Blanca Canales raise the Puerto Rican flag during the October 30, 1950 Jayuya Uprising. Arrested days later, he was sentenced to life and served about nine years at La Princesa prison in San Juan before his release amid international pressure, and he later chronicled the uprising in his memoir "Coabey: el valle heroico."

The campaign — sparked by the April 19, 1999 death of civilian Navy security guard David Sanes Rodríguez when an errant Marine F/A-18 bomb struck his observation post — drew Puerto Ricans of every political stripe (independentistas, statehooders, the Catholic Church, fishers, environmentalists) into a sustained nonviolent direct-action campaign demanding the Navy leave Vieques. Defendants were prosecuted in U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) and typically served 30 to 90 days in federal custody, most often at MDC Guaynabo. The Navy formally ceased operations on Vieques on May 1, 2003. Listed as a current prisoner in Nuclear Resister Issue #121 "Inside & Out" prisoner roster.

expected.description:
Convicted in U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) for participating in the School of the Americas Watch (SOA Watch) annual nonviolent civil-disobedience action at Fort Benning, Georgia on September 2002. Defendants typically received 3 to 6 months in federal custody plus a fine.

Thomas Mahedy crossed the line at Fort Benning, Georgia during the November 2001 SOA Watch vigil to close the U.S. Army School of the Americas / WHINSEC. Sentenced to 3 months in federal custody.

Each year on the November anniversary of the assassination of six Jesuits, their housekeeper, and her daughter at the University of Central America in San Salvador in 1989, peace activists gather at the gates of Fort Benning, Georgia, site of the U.S. Army School of the Americas / Western Hemisphere Institute for Security Cooperation (WHINSEC), to commemorate the dead and to call for the school's closure. Hundreds have crossed the line onto the base over four decades of vigils; many have served federal sentences ranging from 30 days to a year for trespass.

operations.name: Wesley Everest

expected.name: Wesley Everest
expected.description: Wesley Everest was an IWW Wobbly, lumber worker, and World War I infantry veteran. On Armistice Day, November 11, 1919, American Legion marchers attacked the Centralia, Washington IWW union hall. Everest was inside; in the resulting gunfight four Legionnaires were killed. Everest fled, was captured, and was held in the Centralia city jail. That night a mob took him from the jail, castrated him in the back of a car en route to the Chehalis River, and hanged him from the Mellen Street railroad bridge. The mob then fired on the body. The official coroner's verdict was that Everest "jumped from the bridge with a rope around his neck" — no one was ever prosecuted for his murder. Everest's body was buried by IWW prisoners (the Centralia 8) in an unmarked grave.

expected.name: Ralph DiGia
expected.description: Ralph DiGia was a New York City accountant and lifelong pacifist who refused to register for the draft in World War II. Convicted in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York; served three years of a 3-year federal sentence (1942-1945) at federal prison camps including Lewisburg, Danbury, and Petersburg. Co-founded the War Resisters League's full-time staff after release; participated in the 1947 "Journey of Reconciliation" (precursor to the Freedom Rides) and the 1951 Paris-to-Moscow peace bicycle ride. Worked at the WRL national office until his death.

expected.body:
First Missouri Peace Planting arrest and chronology limits

The original October-November 1988 Post Amerikan report individually names Dorothy Eber, 63, of Villa Park, Illinois among those arrested at Missouri missile silos on August 15, 1988. That first arrest is now recorded at day precision. The newsletter says most participants went to Bates County Jail, but does not individually establish Eber's prison-admission day. A November 9 letter signed by Dorothy and other defendants says they were then out on bond awaiting sentencing. November 9 is therefore a status snapshot, not an exact discharge date and not release from her later federal sentence. The formerly entered March 8, 1956 birth date is removed because it is incompatible with this contemporary account of her age; no replacement birthday is guessed. The existing photograph's provenance is still under review and is not certified by this chronology correction.

Sources: Post Amerikan, October-November 1988, printed page 6 (physical page 7); Post Amerikan, December 1988-January 1989, printed pages 12-13 (physical pages 13-14), defendants' November 9 letter. Complete relevant pages visually inspected.

operations.name: Robert P. Stover

expected.name: Robert P. Stover
expected.description: Robert P. Stover, better known to friends and fellow workers as "Ed" Stover, was an Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) member and Bay Area anarchist organizer arrested in 1970 along with co-defendant Mike Lamm in a wave of anti-leftist police raids targeting Bay Area anarchists. The arrests featured large spreads in the local press with photographs of literature and weapons seized from anarchist homes and a heavily publicized high-speed police chase. Stover and Lamm faced a battery of charges including arson, robbery, receiving stolen weapons, and attempted murder. At the time of his arrest Stover was active in the anti-war and anti-draft movements on both the East and West coasts and was working to build organizing contacts between union militants and the student movement. Stover spent sixteen months in pretrial detention, unable to meet what supporters described as excessively high bail. Mike Lamm raised his own bail but, as the Chicago Anarchist Black Cross Bulletin reported in 1972, "depression over constant harassment of state and federal authorities drove him to jump into San Francisco Bay, where he died." A national Stover-Lamm Defence Fund was organized, and the General Defence Committee of the IWW raised additional money, but Stover was ultimately convicted and sentenced to a very lengthy prison term. He was held at San Quentin State Prison, initially incommunicado and moved frequently. While incarcerated he wrote essays published in the IWW's "Industrial Worker," studied labor law and National Labor Relations Board procedures, prepared his own appellate briefs, and worked on a book titled "Anarchist in Exile."

operations.name: Carl Ahlteen

expected.name: Carl Ahlteen
expected.description:
Carl Ahlteen was editor of the IWW Swedish language newspaper Alarm. According to aDepartment of Justice memorandum, Ahlteen was convicted and sentenced to twenty years at Leavenworth merely for publishing an article in Alarm that opposedU.S. intervention in World War I. In relevant part Ahlteen wrote: War, war, and again war, is the cry. What would a State with its brutal machinery do if the working class absolutely said that they would not transport one pound of food to such beings, who have taken as their business the murdering of others, whether it is our country's or other countries' soldiers. After five years in jail Ahlteen and two other leading Swedish organizers for the IWW, Sigfrid Stenberg and Ragner Johannsen, accepted the commutation of their sentences conditionedupon their deportation from the United States. Each defendanthad to swear that he would ''never return " to this country.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Editor of the Swedish-language IWW paper Allarm beginning in 1915, and a personal friend of Joe Hill. Arrested in Minneapolis in 1917 and convicted in the federal IWW mass trial; sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment and a $20,000 fine. Studied homeopathy while in prison. Released from Leavenworth in 1923 on condition of deportation; deported January 13, 1923.

In Sweden he joined the syndicalist Sveriges Arbetares Centralorganisation and spoke at a 1924 memorial meeting for Joe Hill. Later abandoned labor activism, practiced homeopathy in Stockholm, and was convicted of malpractice in 1933 following several patients’ deaths. Subsequently moved to Colombia and the Panama Canal Zone, where he continued his practice until his death in 1948. His widow and son subsequently relocated to California, and interred his ashes in Oakland.

Anderson was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to five years in prison and fined $30,000. His Leavenworth imprisonment began September 7, 1918, but was interrupted by bond release on September 12, 1919. He later returned to prison and was paroled June 30, 1922. Anderson joined the IWW in 1917 and was hired as a press agent during the Fortina River drivers strike in Montana. After his arrest in Chicago, Anderson awaited trial in the Cook County (Illinois) Jail, where he suffered a physical breakdown and contracted tuberculosis. After returning to Leavenworth, Anderson petitioned for release. His spirit and health broken, Anderson wrote: "bitter experience and grim facts have brought a shocking disillusionment and convinced me of the utter futility of a continued sacrifice and suffering, shut away from life, liberty and love for what I once held dear as an ideal." Anderson was paroled on June 30, 1922. According to an FBI report on his post-prison activities, Anderson never regained good health. His tuberculosis worsened, and, in 1924, he was committed to the Montana State Hospital for the Insane. Local authorities informed the FBI that he was "far gone with tuberculosis" and would die very soon. The FBI's reaction to Anderson's condition was blunt: "As this disposes of this IWW probably permanently, the matter will be considered closed."
expected.body:
1920s custody-date review: The federal report identifies Olin B. Anderson, Leavenworth number 13149, as released on bond 1919-09-12, then returned after 603 days outside prison. The initial and later terms are separated. Neither a later parole eligibility date nor a calculated return day is substituted for an observed custody event.

Source: Government Prosecutions under the Espionage Act (1922), pages 77-78.

operations.name: Giovanni Baldazzi

expected.name: Giovanni Baldazzi
expected.description:
Giovanni Baldazzi was sentenced to ten years in prison. He served in Leavenworth Penitentiary from August 30, 1918, to December 1921, when he was granted clemency and deported.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Active in Italian anarchist circles by 1903, he wrote for several anarchist papers and advocated the general strike. Repeatedly arrested for labor activism, he shifted in 1906 toward individualist anarchism and spent 1907–1910 moving between England, France, and Italy as a sales representative. Expelled from France in 1912, he again engaged in labor struggles in Italy. In 1914 he collaborated on Utopia, a pro-war, syndicalist-leaning newspaper edited by then-socialist Benito Mussolini.

Migrating to the United States later that year, he joined the IWW, became an organizer for its Bakers’ Union in New York, and contributed to (and later edited) the IWW’s Italian-language newspaper Il Proletario. Arrested in Pennsylvania in 1917 for “pernicious activities” and opposition to conscription, he was a defendant in the 1918 federal IWW trial and received a sentence of ten years and a $30,000 fine. His sentence was commuted in 1922 on condition of deportation on February 21, 1922.

Back in Italy, Baldazzi gravitated to Fascist institutions—working for the Opera Nazionale Dopolavoro and later the fascist newspaper La Stirpe—though he never joined the National Fascist Party. 1931–1936 employed as a translator for the Italian National Olympic Committee and the Federazione Internazionale dei Tecnici Agricoli. In 1935, however, he was placed under government surveillance as a suspected antifascist. He began advocating for a liberal-democratic renewal in Europe and petitioned unsuccessfully to emigrate to France in 1936. Died in 1940.

expected.description:
Morris Becker was an anarchist and a vegetarian from New York, New York. Morris Becker was sentenced to a year and eight months in prison. Becker was deported after being rearrested in December 1918 for failing to register for the draft.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Supporter of Alexander Berkman’s The Blast and participated in the No-Conscription League. One of the first individuals arrested under the Selective Service Act of 1917, he received a sentence of one year and eight months in the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary for interfering with the draft. He described himself as “a man without a country,” an anarchist, and “an advocate of peace and not of force.” Deported on the Buford on January 21, 1919.

In Petrograd he secured factory employment but complained of poor conditions, prompting accusations that he was a “pampered bourgeois” nostalgic for “capitalist America.” After a decade of silence, he sent a coded letter to Alexander Berkman in 1931.

expected.description:
J. H. Beyer was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago and served in Leavenworth Penitentiary. Beyer jumped bail pending the appeal of his conviction and became a fugitive from the law. He is said to have taken refuge in Soviet Russia.

Before the Chicago prosecution he was one of the 74 IWW members held in the Snohomish County jail and charged with murder after the Everett Massacre of November 5, 1916, when Sheriff Donald McRae and a posse of armed vigilantes opened fire on the steamer Verona at the Everett dock, killing at least five Wobblies. The charges against all 74 were dropped after Thomas H. Tracy’s acquittal on May 5, 1917. At the time of the massacre he was 56, a painter, born in Michigan.

expected.description: David T. Blodgett was from Des Moines, Iowa. David T. Blodgett was indicted for circulating a speech by Senator Thomas E. Watson of Georgia that criticized the conscription law. Convicted and sentenced to twenty years in prison for anti-war writings, Blodgett served in Atlanta and Leavenworth Penitentiaries from January 11, 1918, to January 7, 1922. At Leavenworth Penitentiary he had a breakdown and was transferred to St. Elizabeth's Hospital for the Insane on January 4, 1919. On February 25, 1920, after being confined at St. Elizabeth's for over a year, Blodgett was transferred to Atlanta Penitentiary. Outraged by the treatment meted out to Blodgett, Senator Watson introduced a bill in the Senate on October 20, 1921, calling for Blodgett's release. Blodgett's sentence was commuted on January 7, 1922.

expected.name: Earl Browder
expected.description: Earl Browder was a trade union activist from Kansas City, Missouri. In 1917, Browder was convicted of failure to register for the draft and conspiracy to interfere with the draft. He served two years in prison at the Bates County Jail in Butler, Missouri, and at Leavenworth Penitentiary. Soon after his release from prison in November 1920, Browder joined the Communist Party. He became a full member of the party's Executive Committee in 1922 and rose to its leadership in the 1930s during the party's most influential period in U.S. history. He served as general secretary from 1934 to 1945, but was stripped of his office in 1945. In 1946, Browder was expelled from the party and labelled a "renegade and revisionist."
expected.body:

The entry date is recorded as a day, but the release date only as a month: November 1 is a storage placeholder, not a documented release day. His earlier county-jail confinement and intervening time at liberty are not included in this Leavenworth interval.

Source: Joseph North, Earl Browder: A Profile, New Masses, April 30, 1935, pages 13-14. Original scanned pages inspected. An advance announcement of surrender is not substituted for the reported prison-entry date.

operations.name: Lotta Burke

expected.name: Lotta Burke
expected.description:
Lotta Burke was a Cincinnati garment worker, labour leader, suffragist, Socialist, pacifist and women's-rights speaker. Sources give her dates as 1869-1960, while a contemporary report called her 45 in June 1917, which would place her birth around 1871 or 1872; neither establishes an exact birth date, so none is recorded. A later biographical account says she died in December 1960 and was buried at St. John Cemetery in St. Bernard, Ohio.

She was arrested in Cincinnati on June 12, 1917 with Thomas Hammerschmidt, initially on a treason allegation, for ordering anti-conscription handbills. After a preliminary hearing on June 25 she was held in a Dayton, Ohio jail and released on July 16 on a $3,000 bond -- a stay of about three weeks.

She was later prosecuted with twelve others for conspiracy to defraud the United States by encouraging men not to register for military service, and was convicted by February 1920. A government compilation records a fifteen-month sentence and names Missouri State Prison, but no admission or release has been found and she was on appeal bond during the litigation. The Sixth Circuit affirmance was reported in 1923.

ON MAY 26, 1924 THE SUPREME COURT REVERSED ALL THIRTEEN CONVICTIONS, holding that openly urging resistance to draft registration was not defrauding the United States under the statute charged.

An earlier version of this record said she served fifteen months in the Missouri State Prison. Fifteen months was the sentence imposed; whether she served any of it is unresolved.

operations.name: Ralph Chaplin

expected.name: Ralph Chaplin
expected.description:
Ralph Chaplin was from Chicago, Illinois. Ralph Chaplin was sentenced to twenty years in prison at the IWW trial in Chicago. Chaplin was a songwriter and editor of the IWW's banner newspaper Solidarity. His most famous song, "Solidarity Forever, " remains popular as the anthem of the trade union movement. Chaplin served in Leavenworth Penitentiary from September 1918 to July 1919 and from April 1921 until the commutation of his sentence on June 25, 1923. The Department of Justice initially recommended against any reduction of sentence, calling Chaplin a "notorious agitator" who used "all his power and influence to belittle the government." At Leavenworth the warden criticized Chaplin as a "lazy, " "sneaking" and "double dealing" prisoner: Chaplin is more cunning than the average IWW prisoner and he tries sneaking ways to get others to make trouble for the prison officials... Chaplin poses as a poet and is a lazy loafer. During his incarceration Chaplin's family and friends published a chapbook of prison poems.

Ralph Hosea Chaplin IWW's leading songwriter, poet, and propagandist; wrote "Solidarity Forever" on January 17, 1915, set to "John Brown's Body." Joined IWW 1913; in 1916 became editor of the union's eastern paper Solidarity. Convicted in the 1918 Chicago mass trial; sentenced to 20 years and a $30,000 fine. Served roughly four years at Leavenworth before Harding's December 1923 amnesty. Chronicled prison years in "Bars and Shadows" (1922) and autobiography "Wobbly" (1948).

operations.name: Frederick Esmond

expected.name: Frederick Esmond
expected.description: Frederick Esmond was an Oxford University graduate. Frederick Esmond was a newspaper and publicity agent for the IWW. Esmond headed the California Defense Committee for the Sacramento IWW Sedition Act defendants. After protesting the prison conditions endured by the Sacramento defendants to the U.S. attorney general, Esmond was himself arrested and charged with sedition. He was held in isolation for eight months and then tried along with the other "silent defendants" in Sacramento and sentenced to ten years. Esmond responded to the announced convictions by shouting: we, the outcasts, have been framed up, clubbed, beaten, slugged, martyred, and murdered. Is it any wonder that I do not consider myself bound to your procedures when this court and its proceedings are a disgrace to the United States? Esmond never recovered from the weakened state of health caused by his pre-trial confinement in isolation. He entered Leavenworth Penitentiary on January 25, 1919. On April 7, 1921, he suffered a complete mental collapse—becoming "maniacal, noisy, destroying clothing and bedding." According to the prison physician, Esmond reportedly started to have "delirious hallucinations" and became "homicidal." The physician attributed Esmond's breakdown to "overwork of his mental facilities, accompanied by worry and depression." Esmond was transferred to St. Elizabeth's Hospital where he slowly recuperated. He was pardoned and released from the asylum in February 1923.

expected.description: Flora I. Foreman was an Oregon Socialist and schoolteacher prosecuted under the Espionage Act in Texas. In a prison letter dated November 20, 1918, she reported being arrested June 3 and held because she could not furnish bond. She was tried and sentenced to five years on October 16, 1918.
