expected.body:
1920s custody review: Foreman's own letter dated November 20, 1918, published in The Liberator, January 1919, page 3, explicitly dates her arrest June 3, 1918 and describes detention because she could not furnish bond. It dates her trial, conviction and five-year sentence October 16, 1918; this was not her admission to McAlester. The letter says transfer to that prison was still anticipated. Accordingly October 16 is moved from prison admission to sentencing. Her June 3 jail detention is documented here, but an uninterrupted interval through the existing June 17, 1922 release has not been established. The inherited release date is retained pending independent verification, and no exact total is asserted. The phrase physical wreck describes her condition in November 1918, not necessarily her condition upon release. Existing identified photograph retained.

Source: Foreman prison letter

expected.description:
Frank Geizler was an Austrian member of the Industrial Workers of the World. He was held at Grand Forks, North Dakota by September 1, 1917, prosecuted at Fargo for threatening President Woodrow Wilson, and sentenced to two years, which he is reported to have begun serving on March 9, 1918 at the United States Penitentiary at Leavenworth as prisoner number 12495.

On October 18, 1919 he was re-arrested by police immediately upon his release from Leavenworth and held for deportation. The final deportation disposition and the detention facility are unresolved.

The interval from March 9, 1918 to October 18, 1919 is 588 days. That figure is calculated from the two reported dates rather than taken from any statement of time served, and it excludes the unresolved pre-trial custody at Grand Forks.

Voetter were arrested on December 22 last while carrying dynamite. The year is therefore 1917. The complete original page was visually checked. Contemporary individual date evidence

This is attributed secondary evidence; no original discharge-register day is claimed. The December 22, 1923 Commercial and Financial Chronicle reports the December 15 commutation and forthcoming release warrants, not physical departure, and therefore is not used to infer a release day. Kohn December 1917 pretrial beginning is not copied as Leavenworth admission.

operations.name: Burt Lorton

expected.name: Burt Lorton
expected.description:
Burt Lorton was a nine-year IWW member and secretary of its Chicago Recruiting Union. Burt Lorton was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago for seditious conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct military service. He was sentenced on August 30, 1918, to ten years in prison and fined $30,000. He served in the Cook County Jail and Leavenworth Penitentiary from September 7, 1917, to December 24, 1923.

Although Lorton was arrested for obstructing enlistment, confidential Department of Justice documents admit that "[n]o evidence was adduced, either oral or otherwise showing that [he] had written, said or done anything against the war." Nevertheless, the Department of Justice urged against releasing Lorton because of his eminence in the trade union leadership: " The Metal Machinery Workers Union had gained a decided increase in members because of his agitation." Lorton was placed in permanent segregation because of continuous conflicts with the prison administration. Among the pages of disciplinary write-ups, guards complained ferociously: Yesterday [Lorton] said he knew several persons who did not have the nerve to steal but made their living standing over prisoners with a club. This was intended as an insult.... [Action taken: ] Placed in isolation on restricted diet. After being notified to break rock smaller, he just looked up and laughed.... [Action taken: ] Reprimanded (already in isolation). Throwing dishes and creating a general disturbance in dining room.... [Action taken: ] Segregated indefinitely as a dangerous and irresponsible character. Permanent segregation undermined Lorton's health. According to a letter to Leavenworth Warden A. V. Anderson from Carolina Lowe, an IWW Defense Committee official: When he entered the penitentiary, he was strong and sturdy looking, a picture of robust health. When I saw him the other day, he looked like a different man, he looked so pale and has lost many pounds, I am sure, in weight.

operations.name: Enrique Flores Magon

expected.name: Enrique Flores Magon
expected.description:
Enrique Flores Magon was an anarchist publisher from Mexico City, Mexico. Enrique Flores Magon was convicted of "mailing non-mailable matter " (i.e., Mexican revolutionary material) and was sentenced to three years in prison. He served in McNeil Island and Leavenworth Penitentiaries from May 21, 1918, to September 10, 1920. His brother Ricardo Magon died in Leavenworth Penitentiary on November 21, 1922. (See also Chapters 6 and 14.) Magon published the newspaper Regeneracion with his brother. The FBI categorized the Magon brothers as "very prominent in the International Anarchist Movement " for having published articles "worldwide." They were both expelled from Mexico by General Porfirio Diaz for their opposition activities and settled in the United States. While in this country Enriqueremained active in radical and Mexican revolutionary activities. The Magon brothers' newspaper Regeneracion was suppressed by the government at the outbreak of World War I. After Enrique Magon's release from Leavenworth the Department of Justice's Bureau of Investigation carefully monitored his activities. William Burns, the bureau's director, concluded that Magon was "responsible for the greater portion of anarchistic activities" in Los Angeles and instructed the bureau to " immediately " prepare materials to justify his deportation. Thebureau was particularly upset with an " OpenLetter " Magon published shortly after his release from prison, where he wrote: [T]his ill called Country of Liberty has now converted into a crime punishable by twenty years in the Penitentiary anyone who preaches free thought and free speech. Thousands upon thousands of men and women have come under the law, merely for having sufficient valor to attack the ruling tyranny.... I must now ask you, must we remain indifferent before such outrages? TheDepartment of Justice continued to monitor Magon andon October 11, 1922, hadhim arrested onadeportation warrant. Thecourt ruled that he was an "alien anarchist " who "knowingly distributes" " printedmatter " " teaching opposition to all organized government. " On March 21, 1923, Magon, his wife and four children were deported to Mexico.

Enrique Flores Magón was briefly jailed in San Antonio, Texas, around 1904 following a politically charged confrontation, and was later arrested in connection with the Partido Liberal Mexicano press. Exact dates are incomplete.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Opposed the dictatorship of Mexican president Porfirio Díaz, along with his brother Ricardo Flores Magón, leading to their arrests in 1903. Later that year the brothers immigrated to the United States, where they founded the Partido Liberal Mexicano (PLM) and its newspaper Regeneración.

Over time, the PLM became increasingly radical, embracing anarchism and supporting the IWW. Enrique was repeatedly arrested in the US for political activities. In 1917 he broke with the PLM over personal and political disagreements. In 1918 began serving a sentence for “mailing unmailable matter” and was released from Leavenworth Penitentiary in 1920. On March 4, 1923 he accepted “voluntary departure” to Mexico. 

Remained active in Mexican anarchist circles and wrote for the international anarchist press through 1926, when he announced his “retirement” from the movement due to physical disability and poverty. In the 1930s accepted a government pension as a “precursor of the Mexican Revolution” and dedicated himself to rewriting the history of the PLM as part of the history of Mexican nationalism. Died in 1954.

operations.name: J. Emma Martin

expected.name: J. Emma Martin
expected.description: J. Emma Martin, a Bible Student in San Bernardino, was prosecuted under the Espionage Act and sentenced on July 31, 1918 to three years. An institutional history reports her March 1918 arrest and her return to custody on May 17, 1920 after appeals. She served at San Quentin. Her sentence was commuted June 21, 1920; her release is documented to 1920, but the exact physical discharge day remains unresolved.
expected.body:
1920s custody review: The Senate table identifies July 31, 1918 as sentencing, not prison admission, and June 21, 1920 as commutation to expire at once. The Watchtower institutional retrospective reports arrest a few days after the March 17, 1918 meeting, and entry to serve sentence on May 17, 1920 after appeals. Arrest is therefore recorded only to March 1918, and admission as May 17, 1920 with that retrospective attribution. The reproduced San Bernardino County Sun clipping of June 27, 1920 still describes an order for immediate release, rather than documenting the physical discharge. The retrospective places the end of imprisonment in 1920; the structured release field is left blank pending a physical discharge date, not automatically set to June 21 or June 27. A year-only date would sort before the known May admission in the current storage format. The former July 31, 1921 release and three-year duration were unsupported arithmetic. Earlier pretrial detention and bail are not treated as uninterrupted prison time. The inherited Carson City assertion is not substantiated by these sources; they identify the southern California prosecution and San Quentin custody. Existing photograph retained.

Sources: 1921 Senate hearing, page 89, original table visually inspected; Watchtower, October 2020 retrospective; Reproduced contemporary newspaper clipping, visually inspected.

operations.name: Dr. Walter A. Matthey

expected.name: Dr. Walter A. Matthey
expected.description: Dr. Walter A. Matthey was a Davenport, Iowa physician. Dr. Walter A. Matthey helped arrange a July 25, 1917 meeting at which Daniel H. Wallace delivered an anti-war and anti-conscription speech. Matthey distributed pamphlets announcing the address, attended and applauded, and reportedly contributed 25 cents. An attorney-general clemency summary later described the case as no more than attending, listening, applauding statements whose exact nature was supposedly unknown, and contributing a quarter, but the Eighth Circuit cited more: he helped organize the meeting, handed out the pamphlets previewing the speech, and applauded, so that his participation was not merely accidental. Federal authorities convicted him in October 1918 of aiding and abetting an attempt to cause insubordination, disloyalty and refusal of military duty. He received one year and one day in Leavenworth Penitentiary and a $1,000 fine. The Eighth Circuit affirmed the conviction on August 10, 1921, and the Supreme Court declined review in January 1922. His best reconstructed imprisonment dates are approximately April 3, 1921 to April 3, 1922 — the entry date is inferred from the sentence length and a federal report giving April 4, 1922 as the scheduled expiration of the term, and still requires confirmation from the Leavenworth admission register. A published chronology placing him at Leavenworth continuously from October 18, 1918 cannot be right for a sentence of a year and a day whose appeals ran into 1922. President Warren G. Harding formally pardoned him on or about April 6, 1922, without canceling the fine. One later secondary source gives his middle initial as C., but contemporary medical reporting and newspaper accounts use Walter A. Matthey.

operations.name: John Alex MacDonald

expected.name: John Alex MacDonald
expected.description:
John Alex MacDonald was the editor of the Industrial Worker. John Alex MacDonald received a ten-year sentence, of which he served over five years in Leavenworth Penitentiary. In prison he became a schoolteacher, but lost that position and was sent into isolation for "becoming sarcastic and ridiculing the laws and system of Government of the United States." He described his prison experience in harsh language: Depicted by a Milton or a Dante, Hell had its flashes of sulphur, its massive pictures of damnation; here also is damnation, but it is a damnation sordid, soiled, small, unpicturesque and mouldy as a decaying corpse.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Served nine years in the US Army at Vancouver, Washington, before discharge due to tuberculosis contracted during service. He joined the IWW around 1913 in Kansas City and became editor of The Industrial Worker in Seattle in May 1916, actively defending members prosecuted after the Everett Massacre. A defendant in the federal IWW trial (1917–1918), he was sentenced to ten years. His wife Kate (Katherine Beidel), whom he married in 1918, edited the paper during the trial until July 1918. His sentence was commuted in 1923, and he was deported to Canada August 5, 1923.

In Canada he continued organizing for the IWW and writing for its US publications through at least 1926, including organizing agricultural workers alongside fellow deportee Sam Scarlett.

MacDonald was diagnosed with a mild case of tuberculosis, but the government refused to grant clemency because he had published the poem “A Patriot” in the Industrial Worker: “I love my country, yes, I do, / I love my Uncle Sam, / I also love my steak and eggs, / I guess I won’t enlist. / I love my flag, I do, I do, / Which floats upon the breeze, / I also love my arms, and legs, / I guess I won’t enlist. / I love my country, yes, I do, / I hope her folks do well; / Without our arms and legs and things / I think we’d look like Hell. / Yet men with faces half shot off / Are unfit to be seen; / I’ve read in books it spoils their looks, / I guess I won’t enlist.”

operations.name: Louis Parenti

expected.name: Louis Parenti
expected.description:
Louis Parenti was a laborer from San Francisco, California. Louis Parenti was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to five years in prison and fined $30,000. Parenti was imprisoned from September 1917 to June 1919 and from May 1921 to August 12, 1922, when his sentence was commuted on the condition that he would be deported. He had a wife and three children. He served in the Cook County Jail and Leavenworth Penitentiary. During his first fifteen months in prison Parenti was unable to contact his wife, Marie. During that time she gave birth to a baby girl and wrote to the warden describing her condition: Pardon me for taking the liberty to write. Days and nights I have had no rest. Since my husband has been in this prison I haven't received a single line from him.... I am a mother of three poor children and I have suffered all the tortures in the world. And also since my husband has been away we have born a baby girl that my husband has never seen. I had a big operation which I suffered a whole lot and I had to abandon for 4 weeks the children at home. I would beg you to allow my husband... to write a few lines to his wife. At about the same time Parenti asked the warden to approve the following telegram to his wife: " I wish news my wife about you and little daughters. Tell me the truth. Kisses." On May 21, 1921, the Parentis were granted permission to communicate with each other.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Initially a Christian democrat and completed two years of seminary study in Lucca before abandoning religious training, marrying, and assisting an Italian streetcar drivers’ strike. 

He emigrated to the United States with his wife Maria in 1910 and soon became an anarchist, joining the Industrial Workers of the World in San Francisco in 1911. He became a lecturer and organizer for the IWW and was arrested several times for leading strikes and demonstrations. Italian consular authorities described him as “one of the most dangerous propagandists in the anarchist movement across the United States,” calling him “taciturn in character, educated, intelligent, [and] cultured.” A defendant in the mass IWW trial of 1917–1918, he was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment and a $30,000 fine. From September 1917 to June 1919 he was denied permission to communicate with his wife and three daughters, one of whom was born while he was incarcerated. Released on bail pending appeal, he worked as an organizer for an independent Italian fishermen’s union in San Francisco and later as a correspondent for La Voce del Popolo. After losing his appeal in May 1921, he reentered prison, but in 1922 his sentence was commuted on condition of deportation. He “voluntarily departed” with his family on October 26, 1922.

Back in Italy, he settled in Lucca, joined the syndicalist Unione Sindacale Italiana, and attended its illegal 1926 convention. He later withdrew from overt radical activity and worked for a Fascist state-created union and as a reporter. Official reports alternately described him as obedient to Fascist directives (1929), secretly receiving radical publications from the United States (1930), and again demonstrating “good moral and political conduct” aligned with the regime (1932). The true nature of his political beliefs in these years is unclear. Died in 1961.

expected.name: Grover H. Perry
expected.description: Grover H. Perry was an Industrial Workers of the World organizer and secretary-treasurer of the Metal Mine Workers Industrial Union in Salt Lake City. An outspoken opponent of U.S. participation in World War I, he was convicted in the 1918 Chicago IWW mass trial, sentenced to twelve years and fined $20,000. Perry was held in the Chicago House of Corrections and Leavenworth Penitentiary, where he developed pulmonary tuberculosis, before his release on bond in September 1919. He did not surrender after the appeal failed and was one of nine defendants identified in IWW records as having left for Soviet Russia in 1921.

operations.name: Edward Quigley

expected.name: Edward Quigley
expected.description: Edward Quigley was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Sacramento and sentenced to ten years in prison. He contracted an especially serious case of tuberculosis at Leavenworth Penitentiary, but was denied adequate medical care and was forced to protest the unsanitary prison hospital conditions. These were so deplorable that even the guards acknowledged them in Quigley's official prison record: "Other men state that the nurse is filthy and handles the thermometer with filthy hands. This is corroborated by practically all patients in the annex." A Department of Justice memorandum stated that Quigley was dying from tuberculosis and both lungs were infected: "An outside physician of high standing states that Quigley will probably not live more than three or four years at the most." Consequently, the pardon attorney recommended a commutation of sentence: "This prisoner is no longer defiant but is subdued and appears to be improved by reason of his imprisonment. He promises to be law abiding in the future" (emphasis supplied). The prison doctor concurred with these opinions, noting that the likelihood of Quigley's recovery was "very doubtful" and that between January and October 1923 Quigley's condition had "appreciably failed." Nevertheless, Quigley was kept in prison for two more months, until December 23, 1923, when his sentence was commuted.

1920s custody-date review: The federal report identifies Edward Quigley, Leavenworth number 13578, as released on bond 1920-03-13, then returned after 419 days outside prison. The initial and later terms are separated. Neither a later parole eligibility date nor a calculated return day is substituted for an observed custody event.

Source: Government Prosecutions under the Espionage Act (1922), pages 77-78.

operations.name: Librado Rivera

expected.name: Librado Rivera
expected.description:
Librado Rivera was an anarchist and copublisher with the Magon brothers of Regeneracion. Librado Rivera was sentenced to fifteen years in prison. He served in McNeil Island and Leavenworth Penitentiaries. After five years in prison Rivera developed rheumatism, pyorrhea and other ailments. He was released from prison and deported to Mexico in October 1923.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): In Mexico, became a teacher in 1888 and in 1900 cofounded a liberal political group in San Luis Potosí opposing Catholic influence on the government. Arrested in 1902 for political activities, he served a year in prison. In 1903 he collaborated with Ricardo Flores Magón and others on El hijo del Ahuizote and was arrested for “ridiculing public officials.” 

After migrating to the United States in 1905, he cofounded the Partido Liberal Mexicano and soon adopted anarchism. Arrested in St. Louis in 1906, the US government attempted unsuccessfully to extradite him to Mexico. In 1907 he moved to Los Angeles, where he and other PLM leaders were arrested without warrants by private detectives acting for the Mexican government and convicted of violating US neutrality laws, though later released. In 1910 he became a founding editor of Regeneración. Arrested again in 1911 for neutrality violations related to organizing PLM fighters for the Mexican Revolution, he was imprisoned until 1914. In 1918 he was convicted under the Espionage Act for material published in Regeneración and sentenced to fifteen years. In 1920 he was transferred from McNeil Island to Leavenworth Penitentiary. His sentence was commuted in 1923 on condition of deportation to Mexico.

Back in Mexico he declined government posts offered in San Luis Potosí and continued publishing anarchist newspapers and supporting anarcho-syndicalist unionxsin Tampico, for which he was arrested repeatedly. He died in 1932 after being struck by a car in Mexico City.

In a letter to his brother, Sandargos described his meeting with Eugene Debs in prison: I see E. V. Debs on Saturday and Sunday afternoons when we are in the yard. I find him a splendid fellow and full of spirit. He will always fight for the workers, no matter where or when. All of the poor fellows here run to him for help. operations.name: Sam Scarlett

expected.name: Sam Scarlett
expected.description:
Sam Scarlett was a machinist and IWW lecturer from Chicago, Illinois. Sam Scarlett was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to twenty years in prison and fined $20,000. He served in Leavenworth Penitentiary from September 7, 1918, to January 31, 1923. Scarlett's sentence was commuted when he agreed to be deported to England and swore never to return to the United States. In 1939, the FBI reopened its files on Scarlett when it was rumored that he had been arrested in Canada for helping to publish certain articles in The Clarion, a pro-communist newspaper in Toronto. Incredibly, the FBI continued its search for Scarlett from 1940, when he was rumored to have died, until 1959, simply to confirm his death. Scarlett's FBI record, released in 1990, was riddled with withheld and deleted pages.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Originally a member of the International Association of Machinists, he was radicalized and joined the Industrial Workers of the World in 1911, becoming a prominent speaker and organizer reportedly arrested about 160 times. Among these arrests was his detention during the 1916 strike on the Mesabi Iron Range on murder charges that were later dropped. A defendant in the federal IWW trial of 1917–1918, he was sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment and a $20,000 fine. His sentence was commuted in 1923 on condition of deportation, and he was deported to England in April of that year.

That August he emigrated to Canada and resumed organizing for the IWW in the Vancouver area, especially among miners. Canadian authorities attempted to deport him in 1924 using evidence supplied by US immigration officials, but the case was dropped. In 1931 he joined the Communist Party of Canada. He became an organizer for the party’s Mine Workers’ Union of Canada and was arrested in connection with the violent Estevan strike of October 1931, receiving a one-year sentence that damaged his health. Around 1938 he became chairman of the party in Toronto and of its newspaper The Clarion. When the party was outlawed in 1940, Scarlett lived underground and clandestinely entered the United States, where he remained illegally until his death in 1941.

operations.name: Stephen Shuren

expected.name: Stephen Shuren
expected.description: Stephen Shuren was arrested in Kansas and scheduled to be tried in the mass IWW trial in Wichita. While awaiting trial Shuren attempted suicide at the Shawnee County Jail in Kansas. The attempted suicide occurred after Shuren had spent approximately a year in jail. After having been forced to share a cell with a seriously syphilitic inmate, Shuren "snapped, " using his shaving razor "to cut a deep wound in his neck from ear to ear, and fell to the floor." Nearly dead he was rushed to the hospital. Wliile recuperating he wrote: "Life has denied me everything. WHiiat have I to live for? W^hy should I live?" Within two weeks of the attempt, he was transferred back to the Shawnee County Jail. His fellow IWW inmates watched over Shuren continuously after his return. A reporter commissioned by the National Civil Liberties Union and Survey magazine visited Shuren and wrote that "the expression in his eyes was not normal and he looked at me from his clouded face. The men said that little of his mind seemed to remain." Shuren was transferred to the state insane asylum at Osawattomie. Soon thereafter the government dropped its indictment of these Wichita IWW defendants.

expected.description:
Sigfrid Stenberg was the manager of the IWW paper Alarm, from Minneapolis, Minnesota. Sigfrid Stenberg was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to ten years in prison and fined $30,000. He served in the Cook County Jail and Leavenworth Penitentiary from September 1917 to November 1919 and from April 1921 to November 1922. Stenberg had a wife and one child. Stenberg was released on the condition that he would be deported to Sweden and never return to the United States.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Born 1892, Sweden. Painter; editor. Migrated to US 1912. Wife and daughter in Sweden. Joined the IWW and became business manager of its Swedish-language newspaper Allarm in Minneapolis. Defendant in federal IWW trial 1917-1918; convicted of violating the Espionage Act and sentenced to ten years in prison and a $30,000 fine. Sentence commuted on condition of deportation; deported January 13, 1923. 

Immediately joined the syndicalist Sveriges Arbetares Centralorganisation (SAC), which he viewed as a direct continuation of his activism on behalf of IWW and “the idea that cannot be downed.” In 1928 he became a journalist for the SAC’s daily newspaper Arbetaren, which he also edited from 1930 to 1940. In addition he served as chairman of Sweden’s Executive Committee of the Newspaper and Printing Federation from 1932 to 1942, and treasurer of the anarcho-syndicalist International Working Men’s Association from 1938 until his death in 1942.

INS file 54616/52

See also: Mark Wyman, Round-Trip to America: The Immigrants Return to Europe, 1880-1930; https://www.sac.se/Om-SAC/Historik/Biografier/Stenberg,-Sigfrid-1892-1942

operations.name: Joshua Sykes

expected.name: Joshua Sykes
expected.description: Joshua Sykes was a pacifist pastor associated with the Church of the Living God in Berkeley, California. His federal conviction was followed by appeals and delayed imprisonment. Historian Andrea Shan Johnson, citing his McNeil Island prison register, records admission on March 27, 1921 and release on June 10, 1922. His religious opposition included resistance to wartime demands for military participation and patriotic observance.
expected.body:
1920s custody review: Andrea Shan Johnson, A Shudder Swept Through Them, Pneuma 38 (2016), pages 326-327 and note 51, distinguishes the conviction and appeals from actual prison admission. Citing McNeil Island entry 3743 (M1619, roll 2), Johnson dates booking March 27, 1921 and release June 10, 1922. The former January 21, 1919 McNeil admission is corrected; that date did not mark the start of his prison term. Earlier arrests and transport detention remain separate unresolved events. The June 29, 1918 Oregon Daily Journal page 7 reports indictment, not an arrest date. Johnson identifies a prison photograph in NARA series 608846, box 13, but the actual image has not yet been retrieved or published.

Source; Source; Source

1920s duration reconciliation: The source-supported interval 1921-03-27 through 1922-06-10 computes to 440 elapsed days (end minus start). This is the specific documented custody episode, not necessarily lifetime custody; earlier or later unquantified detention is excluded. Johnson's scholarly article cites McNeil register entry3743 for March27,1921 booking and June10,1922 discharge.440days supported. The previously blank audit expectation was superseded by this explicit evidence-based calculation; no event dates are changed here.

operations.name: William Tanner

expected.name: William Tanner
expected.description:
William Tanner was from Chicago, Illinois. William Tanner was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to five years in prison and fined $30,000. He served in the Cook County Jail and Leavenworth Penitentiary from December 1917 to May 1919 and from April 1921 to October 27, 1922. Tanner's sentence was commuted on the condition that he would be deported and never return to the United States.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Born 1884, Kuopio, Finland. Mechanic. Migrated to Canada 1911; from there migrated to US in 1912 (though he later mistakenly claimed 1914). Became prominent Finnish member of the IWW; wrote for and edited Finnish-language IWW newspaper. Defendant at the federal IWW trial 1917-18; sentenced to five years in prison. An enthusiastic supporter of the Bolshevik Revolution, he apparently joined the Communist Party of America while in Leavenworth Penitentiary, and by 1919 promoted what he called “Bolshevism-IWWism,” or “industrial communism.” July 1922 his sentence was commuted on the condition of deportation. Because the “Government of Finland may raise objections to receiving this man and might refuse to issue a passport,” he was deported to Russia on the grounds that Finland had been a Russian territory at the time of his birth, and because Russia was willing to issue him a passport. Deported October 31, 1922. Upon his departure Tanner declared: “Deported to Soviet Russia, I will continue fighting under the red flag of the workers’ republic for the crushing of world imperialism and for the building of the republic of work. Long live the class solidarity of the proletariat and the red Internationals.” 1923 migrated to Finland. 1925 became a speaker for the Communist-affiliated Suomen Ammattijärjestö (Finnish Trade Union Confederation) and an organizer for the Communists’ Sosialistinen työväen ja pienviljelijöiden vaalijärjestö (Socialist Electoral Organization of Workers and Smallholders ). 1927-1930 a member of the Finnish Parliament, where he “manifested communist orthodoxy.” In late 1930 he returned to the Soviet Union, where he worked for the Comintern. In 1935 he was a lecturer at the International Lenin School and director of a Moscow watch factory; that same year he was arrested as part of Stalin’s purges and sentenced to five years in the gulag at the White Sea-Baltic Canal for “counter-revolutionary activity”; 1937 transferred to the Ukhta-Izhemsk Camp. Released 1940 and died that same year.

INS file 54616/153

See also: Ancestry.com; Industrial Workers of the World Collection, Walter P. Reuther Library, Wayne State University; Auvo Kostiainen, The Forging of Finnish-American Communism, 1917-1924: A Study in Ethnic Radicalism; Tommi Kippola, “Transnationell syndikalism i ett lokalt rum: Industrial Workers of the World och finländarna i Duluth 1915–1921” https://www.doria.fi/handle/10024/169623; https://fi.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tanner

expected.name: Gustave H. Taubert
expected.description: Gustave H. Taubert, indexed by the National Archives as Gustav H. Taubert, was prosecuted at Concord, New Hampshire for violating espionage laws and imprisoned at Atlanta as inmate 8482. expected.body:
1920s custody review: The Senate hearing lists G. H. Taubert under New Hampshire: sentenced June 6, 1918 to three years, out on expiration August 19, 1919. NARA independently identifies Gustav H. Taubert, Atlanta inmate 8482, Concord, New Hampshire, convicted of violating espionage laws. The former ten-year Chicago-IWW attribution, Leavenworth institution and June 1923 release are corrected. The inherited June 4, 1918 custody-start date is retained provisionally but is not established as Atlanta admission by these sources. No exact duration is asserted.

Sources: 1921 Senate hearing, original table visually inspected; National Archives identity record.

1920s remaining-entry review: Kohn, page 136, dates the beginning of Taubert's sentence to June 4, 1918; the official hearing gives June 6 as sentencing. Pending the Atlanta inmate 8482 register, admission is conservatively recorded as June 1918, without choosing an exact day. June 1 is a month placeholder. The independently documented August 19, 1919 release is unchanged, and no exact duration is asserted.

operations.name: Jacob Tori

expected.name: Jacob Tori
expected.description: Jacob Tori was an IWW delegate and organizer from San Francisco, California. Jacob Tori was indicted by the Department of Justice for his "rantings" against the war and his urging young men "not to register" for the draft. He was convicted at the mass IWW trial in Sacramento and sentenced to ten years in prison, which he served in local county jails and Leavenworth Penitentiary from December 1917 to December 24, 1923. An organizer and a delegate for the IWW since 1913, Tori helped organize the fruit-packing industry. Tori's lack of cooperation in prison caused prison officials to declare him the "most worthless man" at Leavenworth. His twenty written reprimands included offenses such as "killing time, " "indolence and defiance, " "getting up from the supper table without permission, " "wasting food at dinner" and "talking in the mess hall." Twice he was placed in isolation on a restricted diet for being "worthless and insolent." On four occasions he was reprimanded for "refusing to break enough rock." Tori was among the last of the IWW prisoners released on December 24, 1923.

expected.body:
1920s custody review: The Morning Oregonian of May 29, 1917, page 1, carries a Seattle dispatch dated May 28 reporting the arrest that day of Hulet M. Wells and Sam Sadler over anti-draft circulars. It says Wells was released later on a $3,000 bond after a preliminary hearing. May 28, 1917 is added as the original arrest date; this brief initial detention is not continuous imprisonment through 1920. The later prison-admission chronology remains under review: a transcription of the Everett Labor Journal of November 19, 1920 says McNeil admission was June 1919, whereas the inherited database date is March 19, 1918. Original Library of Congress scans were access-blocked during this check, so the disputed admission date is not silently replaced.

Source: Contemporary newspaper report, original page visually inspected.

operations.name: William Weyh

expected.name: William Weyh
expected.description: William Weyh was an IWW leader. William Weyh was convicted of seditious conspiracy at the mass IWW trial in Chicago, sentenced to five years and fined $20,000. He began his term in Leavenworth Penitentiary on September 7, 1918. Weyh contracted tuberculosis at Leavenworth. Despite his tuberculin condition, he was forced to perform hard labor (breaking rocks) until he suffered twelve hemorrhages in a single day. On December 27, 1921, the prison physician notified Warden W. I. Biddle that Weyh's condition was terminal: "He has had several veiy severe pulmonary hemorrhages in the past few days and the case is very liable to terminate fatally at any time." Even this did not persuade the Department of Justice, which refused to pardon Weyh. According to IWW prisoners: [After his December hemorrhages] he was so emaciated as to be scarcely recognizable. It was at this point that a prison official said to him: "I don't believe you have another ten hours to live if you stay in this place. Drop your I.W.W. affiliations, and you can be out of here." Weyh's answer was: "No, I'll die first." Weyh continued to suffer in jail for another year until he agreed to the Department of Justice's demand that he be deported if his tuberculosis was cured. Weyh was released on January 25, 1922, but never recuperated and died from tuberculosis two years later, on March 22, 1924.

operations.name: Louis Allen

expected.name: Louis Allen
expected.description:
Louis Allen was a Los Angeles member of the Industrial Workers of the World, convicted with eight co-defendants under California's Criminal Syndicalism Act and sentenced to an indeterminate term of one to fourteen years. He was imprisoned at Folsom State Prison from December 1921 as prisoner number 12026.

A scholarly history records that guards at Folsom covered his head with a blanket, dragged him from solitary confinement and beat him unconscious, and that complaints were filed with the prison board.

His release date is in conflict by one day. A compilation gives September 11, 1925, while a contemporary newspaper report of September 11 says the release would happen "tomorrow", which would make it September 12. Release is recorded at September 1925 month precision while the conflicting day remains unresolved.

This was a state prosecution. An earlier version of this record classified it as a federal Espionage or Sedition Act case.

The June 1925 labor-press political-prisoner birthday notice lists him at Folsom Prison, Represa, under prisoner number 12026 — matching the number already recorded here — with a June 22 birthday (no birth year is given).
expected.body:
1920s custody review: The Daily Worker of September 12, 1925, page 4, states that Allen was first arrested in Los Angeles in April 1921. Only the month is entered. The same article contradicts itself about release: its opening predicts tomorrow under a September 11 dateline, while later wording gives September 11 expiration. Rather than choose between September 11 and 12, release is now month-only September 1925. The article also describes initial San Quentin confinement before transfer to Folsom; the existing December 1921 Folsom date is not established as first custody. No verified individual photograph located.

operations.name: John Bruns

expected.name: John Bruns
expected.description: John Bruns, also recorded as Brunes, was an IWW lumber worker arrested in 1924 and held in Lassen County Jail. He was convicted under California criminal syndicalism legislation in November 1924 and imprisoned at San Quentin. An initially indeterminate one-to-fourteen-year sentence was fixed at four years by the prison board in December 1925. Historian Ahmed White, citing his prison record and a contemporary release report, gives his release as November 9, 1927.
expected.body:
1920s custody review: The September 10, 1924 Daily Worker, page 4, reports Bruns arrested and held in Lassen County Jail; arrest is added at year precision, not assigned the publication day. Charlotte Anita Whitney in the February 13, 1926 Daily Worker, page 2, dates his conviction to November 1924 and says the prison board fixed a four-year term in December 1925 after an initial one-to-fourteen-year sentence. This contradicts the previous 1925 release. Ahmed White, Under the Iron Heel (2022), page 189 and note 143 on page 295, explicitly gives release on November 9, 1927 and identifies San Quentin prisoner 40054, citing the prison register and Industrial Solidarity of November 23, 1927. That sourced release replaces the 1925 placeholder. White places the conviction in 1925, conflicting with the contemporary 1924 reports; the inherited November 12, 1924 prison-admission date is retained, not shifted to 1925. Earlier county-jail admission and an identifiable photograph remain unresolved.

Sources: Daily Worker, September 10, 1924, page 4; Daily Worker, February 13, 1926, page 2; Ahmed White, Under the Iron Heel, pages 189 and 295. Relevant complete pages visually inspected.

1920s duration reconciliation: The source-supported interval 1924-11-12 through 1927-11-09 computes to 1092 elapsed days (end minus start). This is the specific documented custody episode, not necessarily lifetime custody; earlier or later unquantified detention is excluded. Kohn own entry p158 explicitly gives SanQuentin start November12,1924; White register-based November9,1927 release resolves vague term-expiration endpoint.1092days supported; White's1925 conviction conflict remains noted. The previously blank audit expectation was superseded by this explicit evidence-based calculation; no event dates are changed here.

expected.description: William Burns was arrested in Yosemite National Park for violating the California criminal syndicalism law by organizing for the IWW and "knowingly" becoming a member of the union. He was arrested in April 1923 and served approximately seventeen months in the county jail while awaiting trial. Because he was arrested in a federal park, Burns was tried in federal court. His jury consisted of a bank president, a "real estate shark, " a deputy sheriff, the superintendent of a bonding company and other persons with admitted prejudice against the IWW. Burns received a fifteen-month prison sentence, which he served in Leavenworth Penitentiary from November 1927 until May 14, 1928, when his sentence was commuted by President Calvin Coolidge.

operations.name: J. A. Casdorf

expected.name: J. A. Casdorf
expected.description: J. A. Casdorf was an IWW member from Sacramento. J. A. Casdorf received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in San Quentin from May 6, 1922, to December 5, 1923. Along with codefendant Earl Firey, Casdorf was charged with the crime of being a member of the IWW, an organization that illegally advocated "criminal syndicalism." After the defendants' first two witnesses (P. Beasley and Charles B. La Rue) testified, the witnesses were promptly arrested under the California criminal syndicalism law. Thereafter the prosecuting state attorney declared in the presence of other potential witnesses that "all witnesses who would thereafter take the stand in this case and admit they were paid up members of the IWW in good standing, would be arrested." The defense pleaded that such statements by the prosecution were prejudicial, that "other witnesses" were "intimidated and terrorized so as to render them less efficient as witnesses" and that other prospective witnesses were "scared away." The trial judge overruled these objections, and eventually eight other IWW members who took the stand were arrested. On appeal, the California District Court of Appeals affirmed Casdorf s conviction. The court held that the "propriety" of the district attorney's action was "debatable, " but that he "acted in good faith" merely to "warn" witnesses of the "consequence[s]" of their testimony. The court held that there was "no prejudice to the substantial rights of the defendants." After the Casdorf conviction, the ten witnesses who took the stand on his behalf were all tried and convicted under the criminal syndicalism law. These convictions were also upheld in People v. LaRue, 216 P. 627 (Cal. App. 1923).

expected.description: Tom Connors was an IWW officer. Tom Connors served a prison sentence in San Quentin from June 2, 1925, to Februaiy 1927. Connors was secretary of the IWW General Defense Committee in California. During his criminal syndicalism trial in Maryville, a prospective juror obtained a copy of literature printed by the General Defense Committee. The state of California dropped the criminal syndicalism charge against Connors and tried him for "corruptly attempting to influence a juror." Connors went through three trials on this charge. The scholarly text gives September 29 as the day, but because that is also its newspaper date and the original discharge report has not been inspected, only the month is recorded. The Daily Worker June 21, 1928 page 4 explicitly places Ellis in Folsom, not San Quentin, and anticipates a September expiration; a predicted date is not used as actual release. The inherited November 1919 arrest is marked at month precision, consistent with the biography. Exact first admission and the escape/recapture custody boundaries remain unresolved. operations.name: Lawrence Emery

expected.name: Lawrence Emery
expected.description: Lawrence Emery was from Sacramento. Lawrence Emery was convicted of violating the California Criminal Syndicalism Act because of his role in the Imperial Valley farmer workers strike. He was sentenced to three to forty-two years in prison and served in San Quentin from June 1930 to February 1933. Emery was an organizer for the Marine Transport Workers Industrial Union and a member of the Communist Party. In early 1930, Emery traveled to Imperial Valley as an organizer for the Trade Union Unity League and began organizing a farm worker strike. The 1930 strike was not successful. Among the demands pushed by the union were an eight-hour work day, abolition of child labor, equal pay for equal work and an end to race segregation among the employees. Because of the strike activities, Emeiy, along with thirty-two others, was indicted under the California Criminal Syndicalism Act. Eventually, eight defendants stood trial and were convicted. The judge presiding at the trial was extremely hostile to the defendants. In a letter to the parole board the judge wrote: "The Court considers the defendants... a decided menace and detriment to society and civilization."

expected.description:
Earl Firey was an IWW member from Sacramento. Earl Firey received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in Folsom from February 17, 1922, to 1925. (See also the entry for J. A. Casdorf.)

A scholarly history identifies him as 27 years old during his spring 1922 prosecution, which — his February birthday having passed — establishes an 1895 birth year; the prisoner birthday list gives the day as February 26 while a genealogy index gives February 29, 1895, a date that cannot exist (1895 was not a leap year), so the birth date is entered at month precision pending confirmation. A Sacramento IWW carpenter, he was convicted of criminal syndicalism with fellow Wobbly J. A. Casdorf and received a five-year sentence, imprisoned from February 17, 1922 — first at San Quentin under number 37474, later at Folsom as 12640 — and released sometime in 1925; the exact date remains unresolved.

operations.name: James P. Gordon

expected.name: James P. Gordon
expected.description:
James P. Gordon was from Los Angeles. James P. Gordon received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in Folsom from July 12, 1923, until his term expired.

P. J. Gordon was imprisoned at Folsom State Prison during the era of California's criminal-syndicalism prosecutions, which sent more than a hundred IWW members and labor radicals to San Quentin and Folsom on one-to-fourteen-year terms. He appears on the International Labor Defense's rosters of American class-war prisoners in Labor Defender (1926-27); like most of the rank-and-file labor prisoners of the period, little else about his case entered the historical record.

The contemporary prisoner birthday list gives his birthday as February 13 (no birth year has surfaced). His prisoner number was 38113 — the 88113 rendered by the optical scan of the list was an error. Sentenced to five years under the California criminal-syndicalism campaign, he entered Folsom on July 12, 1923 and apparently remained until his term expired.

expected.description: Karl Lesse, also known as Charles or Carl Lesse, was a German-born sailor and IWW delegate. He was arrested in February 1919 and released on bail, then rearrested in Arcata, California, in November 1919. Convicted under the state criminal syndicalism law, he received a one-to-fourteen-year sentence and entered San Quentin in January 1920. The cited biography places his release and deportation in 1922 but gives inconsistent March and May dates. In Germany he joined the syndicalist FAUD and then the Communist Party, later working for the Communist International in Europe and Shanghai. That source gives incompatible March and May endpoints, so release is recorded only at year precision; no exact release or deportation day is asserted.

Source: Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees, Charles Lesse.

expected.body:
1920s remaining-entry review: Kohn, American Political Prisoners, page 165, explicitly identifies Thomas O'Mara as the Sacramento IWW defense witness and states that his San Quentin term ran from August 25, 1923 to 1926. The structured release year 1925 conflicted with both this source and the existing biography. It is corrected to 1926 with year precision, explicitly based on secondary historical evidence. The full original Daily Worker page 5 of December 29, 1925 was visually inspected: its prison correspondence directory individually lists Tom O'Mara, number 38293, at San Quentin. That directory supports late-1925 custody but does not establish his release year or prove a discharge day; the 1926 endpoint comes from Kohn. Targeted contemporary searches did not produce an actual discharge report, and White's available book text yielded no individual O'Mara match. An original San Quentin register remains needed for any finer precision. The generic federal-charge label is corrected to the California case identified by Kohn.

operations.name: Fred W. Thompson

expected.name: Fred W. Thompson
expected.description: Fred W. Thompson was an IWW member arrested in Marysville, California, in April 1923. Fred W. Thompson received a four-year prison sentence, which he served in San Quentin from November 7, 1923, to March 7, 1927. In a 1981 letter to the author, Thompson described the experience of the California IWW criminal syndicalism inmates: In San Quentin we wobs went on strike several times (not asking non-wobs to join us) in protest against what we considered unjust discipline to some of our members. Punishment was solitary confinement, not actually solitary—sometimes in the "hole, " underground completely dark but because of our number, putting us two to a cell. Sure that situation was uncomfortable—we had nothing to sit on but the floor, for they took our blanket away at daybreak, and the diet [of] bread and water, and we combatted the sense of isolation—imperfect there because of our numbers—by singing or inventing games. (I recall our efforts for example to list the rivers of North America, starting with the McKenzie and going clockwise, or seeing how far we could go in the dark with the series, 2X3 is 6, 4X6 is 24, 5X24 is 120, 6 times 120 is 720, etc.) Sometimes we were confined on bread and water in a row in the new prison, with daylight, but nothing to read for a month. We had some forbidden pencils and tried making crossword puzzles for each other, sneaking them down the line. Most of us had got in because we stuck our heads out in life outside, and we were an innovative lot of people, better able than most to cope with daily problems. We got along well with the prisoners in on ordinary offenses. I judge that prison conditions have much deteriorated since my days in San Quentin. The food I hear is not as terrible as it was then—weevils in the oatmeal, beans almost every meal, often half cooked—but crowding is worse; radios have worsened life instead of improving it, for one can't get quiet; I heard of no homosexual rape when I was in San Quentin, and I don't believe the prisoners would have permitted it. In general prisoners of all sorts acted with consideration for each other. Thompson remained active in the IWW for his entire adult life and, in 1955, published The I.W.W., Its First Fifty Years.
expected.body:
1920s custody review: In Fellow Worker: The Life of Fred Thompson, edited by David Roediger, Thompson states on printed page 56 that he was arrested in Marysville in April 1923, remained in the local jail through a hung jury and retrial, entered San Quentin on November 7, 1923, and was released March 7, 1927. His December 1940 pardon was a later event, not his release. Printed page 52 identifies his San Quentin number as 38579. The arrest day remains unknown; April 1 is only a month-precision storage placeholder. The existing admission and release dates are independently corroborated, not newly added. The prison interval does not include his earlier local-jail detention.

Source: Fellow Worker: The Life of Fred Thompson, pages 52-56. Original pages visually inspected.

operations.name: Isaac E. Ferguson

expected.name: Isaac E. Ferguson
expected.description: Isaac E. Ferguson was a Canadian-born, Chicago-based attorney and a founding leader of the Communist Party of America in 1919, serving on its Central Executive Committee as International Secretary and party legal counsel. During the First Red Scare he was indicted in New York and, in October 1920, tried jointly with party leader C.E. Ruthenberg in the Supreme Court of New York County under the state's 1902 Criminal Anarchy statute for their role in publishing the "Left Wing Manifesto"; both were convicted on October 29, 1920, sentenced to five years, and Ferguson was imprisoned at Sing Sing. He was released on bond in April 1922, and the New York Court of Appeals reversed both convictions in July 1922 — a companion decision to the landmark Gitlow case — for lack of evidence linking the men to the Manifesto's publication. After his release Ferguson withdrew from radical politics and built a long career as a prominent Chicago attorney; he died in Chicago in 1964. (Recorded as Isaac Edward "Ed" Ferguson)

operations.name: James Larkin

expected.name: James Larkin
expected.description:
James Larkin was born in Liverpool, England. James Larkin was an international leader for Irish independence from Great Britain. Larkin was the general secretary and secretary-treasurer of the Irish Transport and General Workers Union, the largest union in Ireland. Together with James Michael Connolly, he helped lead the Easter Rebellion in Ireland and was subsequently deported. Soon after the outbreak of World War I in Europe, Larkin came to the United States. In 1920, he was convicted of violating the New York criminal anarchy law and sentenced to between five and ten years in jail for his activities in helping found the Communist Party in the United States. After serving approximately two years in jail, he was pardoned by Governor Smith and deported to Ireland.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Raised in poverty in Ireland, Larkin joined the Independent Labour Party in 1893 and became a full-time organizer for the National Union of Dock Labourers in 1905 before being expelled in 1908. He founded the Irish Transport and General Workers’ Union, cofounded the Irish Labour Party in 1912, and helped lead the 1913 Dublin Lockout with James Connolly while also founding the Irish Citizen Army. 

In the United States he joined the Socialist Party of America, aligned with its pro-Bolshevik Left Wing, and lectured widely, often in conjunction with the IWW. Expelled from the SPA in 1919, he cofounded the Communist Labor Party. Arrested under New York’s criminal anarchy law, sentenced to five to ten years, pardoned by Governor Al Smith in 1923, and deported to England in April 1923, after repeated passport denials by British authorities.

Returning to Ireland he founded the Irish Worker League as the country’s official Communist Party and became head of the Communist-aligned Worker’s Union of Ireland. Attended the Fifth Congress of the Comintern in 1924 and appointed to the Comintern’s Executive Committee.In 1927 he was elected to the Irish parliament (Dáil Éireann) on behalf of the IWL , but unable to take his seat due to an unpaid award for libel against him. He resigned from the Comintern in 1929 and broke with Communism completely in 1932. In 1936 he was elected to the Dublin city government; 1937 elected to the Dáil Éireann as an independent candidate, but lost reelection the following year. In 1941 he rejoined the Irish Labour Party and served in the Dáil Éireann from 1943 to 1944. He died in 1947.

operations.name: Frank Burke

expected.name: Frank Burke
expected.description:
Frank Burke was a Socialist conscientious objector from Chicago who was court-martialed after the armistice ending World War I was signed. His death sentence was later commuted to fifteen years in prison. Originally, his prison experiences were typical of other militant Socialists similarly court-martialed: He took part in hunger strikes at Camp Funston, he protested at Fort Leavenworth and was placed in "the hole" on bread and water, and he was subjected to water torture when guards turned powerful fire hoses onto sleeping objectors at Leavenworth. In July 1919, he was transferred from Leavenworth to Fort Douglas. According to contemporary press accounts, Burke was already very sick when he arrived at Fort Douglas on July 10, 1919. Hereported to sick call, sleepless and constipated, but was denied hospitalization until July 25, when his pains reportedly became unbearable. Shortly thereafter a friend visited Burke in the hospital and reported: I found him in pain and unable to retain any food. He had had his stomach pumped out before being moved. I heard from a corps man that Frank had been calling for dope... [An] orderly told me not to bother about Frank's numerous desires, especially his request for a specialist from Salt Lake City.... [Frank] begged me to get a specialist so I went up to see Lieutenant Colonel Graham about getting the services of Major Beer.... Major Beer replied that Frank was suffering, but was in no serious condition and that I could see him the next morning about a specialist. On July 30, 1919, the following day, Frank Burke was dead.

operations.name: James Gossard

expected.name: James Gossard
expected.description: James Gossard was from Urbana, Illinois. James Gossard was arrested and scheduled for trial at the mass IWW trial in Wichita. He was held in the Newton County (Kansas) Jail, where he died while awaiting trial, reportedly because of "improperly treated influenza." 12 Joseph and Michael Hofer (the Hofer brothers) were members of the Hutterite religious order. Their religion forbade cooperation with the military. Sent to Alcatraz, the Hofer brothers refused to obey prison officials and were placed in "the hole." The "hole" was a lightless, rat-infested basement cell. The Hofers were stripped of all their clothing, except underwear, and chained to the walls of this dungeon for eight hours a day. Fed only bread and water and denied proper toilet facilities, their health was broken. They were released from "the hole" and transferred to Fort Leavenworth. Again they refused to work, and although still sick, they were remanded to the Leavenworth solitaiy cell. Within a few days the brothers' condition further deteriorated into pneumonia. They were sent to the prison hospital, where they died.

operations.name: Otto Frederick Schmidt

expected.name: Otto Frederick Schmidt
expected.description: Otto Frederick Schmidt was a twenty-six-year-old member of the IWW arrested in Spokane, Washington. Otto Frederick Schmidt was held for ten months in jail as a deportable alien. Originally detained at an immigration station, Schmidt was arrested without a warrant and held without benefit of a trial or hearing. Schmidt was denied letter-writing privileges and was forced to sleep on a " concrete floor" with "no bed." He fell ill at the immigration station and lost his " teeth and hair. " According to his cellmate, A. George Jensen, Schmidt "believed that the working class should organize to better their conditions. He was arrested for trying to make the world a fit place in which to live." Schmidt was transferred to the Walla Walla County Jail, where conditions remained very poor. When the IWW prisoners collectively protested their condition, the guards responded by hosing them down: A terrific stream of icy cold water was turned onto the sick, half-starved and helpless men, who were locked in a cage, trapped like so many rats. Men were lifted off their feet and battered against the steel bars by the force of the water. Within a few minutes mattresses and blankets were floating about the floor and five men were stretched out, bleeding and unconscious in the wreckage and water. Schmidt was one of the inmates found unconscious after the hosing, but he received no medical attention. His body was merely laid on a " bare iron bunk. " Later, when prison authorities decided he was sufficiently ill to require medical attention, Schmidt was transferred to the Spokane County Jail. But his condition continued to worsen: Schmidt was coughing; the froth was over his drawn lips. During his final days he was removed, sent to the Sacred Heart Hospital, where he died on December 2, 1918.

operations.name: Emil Herman

expected.description: Emil Herman, former Washington State secretary of the Socialist Party, was arrested on April 19, 1918 and prosecuted under the Espionage Act. He was sentenced on June 6, 1918 to concurrent ten-year terms. His confinement was interrupted by bail: after an initial McNeil Island commitment and transfer to Leavenworth, he returned home. Earlier jail periods and bail releases are not combined into one uninterrupted prison term.
expected.body:
1920s custody-date review: June 6, 1918 was the sentencing day, not the initial arrest. Contemporary accounts identify April 19 as the arrest and August 20 as the second McNeil Island admission, after an intervening bail release. The single continuous span has been corrected to that final prison admission; earlier jail episodes are described but not assigned invented endpoints. The existing December 24, 1921 release is retained.

Sources: Debs Freedom Monthly, September 1921, pages 10-11; October 1921, page 18. Original pages visually inspected. An identified photograph of Herman and his wife appears in the September issue; his existing profile photograph is retained.

1920s duration reconciliation: The source-supported interval 1918-08-20 through 1921-12-24 computes to 1222 elapsed days (end minus start). This is the specific documented custody episode, not necessarily lifetime custody; earlier or later unquantified detention is excluded. Kohn own entry p106 explicitly gives December24,1921 release. EarlierJune6 start superseded by primary contemporary August20 final readmission after bail.1222days supported for final episode only. The previously blank audit expectation was superseded by this explicit evidence-based calculation; no event dates are changed here.

operations.name: Marcus Garvey

expected.name: Marcus Garvey
expected.description:
Marcus Garvey was a Jamaican-born Pan-Africanist leader who founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association, the largest Black mass movement in U.S. history, and the Black Star Line shipping company. He was convicted of mail fraud in 1923 in a politically charged federal prosecution related to Black Star Line stock sales and sentenced to five years at Atlanta Penitentiary. President Calvin Coolidge commuted his sentence in 1927 and he was immediately deported to Jamaica, never returning to the United States.

Marcus Mosiah Garvey Jr. Jamaican-born founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (1914) and Black Star Line steamship company (1919). From 1918 the UNIA was a primary target of J. Edgar Hoover's Bureau of Investigation. Federal mail-fraud trial in New York May 18 - June 18, 1923 before Judge Julian W. Mack with Maxwell Mattuck as chief prosecutor. Garvey defended himself; convicted while three co-defendants were acquitted; sentenced to 5 years and $1,000 fine. Served 33 months at U.S. Penitentiary Atlanta before his sentence was commuted by President Calvin Coolidge in November 1927 and he was deported to Jamaica. Posthumously pardoned by President Biden 2025.
expected.body:
1920s custody review: The edited Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers distinguish two custody episodes. Volume IV dates the original mail-fraud arrest to January 12, 1922 (not January 11). Volume V dates sentencing to June 21, 1923 and release on bail from the Tombs to September 10, 1923. The earlier case now represents that detention, with June admission at month precision pending the admission register; it did not continue without interruption to December 1927. Volume VI dates rearrest to February 5, 1925 and Atlanta admission to February 8, 1925, prisoner 19359. It records discharge from Atlanta on November 18, 1927 followed by continued federal custody en route to deportation on December 2. The Atlanta endpoint therefore means prison discharge, not freedom from immigration custody. No record is deleted and no sentence or commutation date is substituted for initial admission.

expected.name: Jim Albertini
expected.description:
Hawaii anti-nuclear and anti-militarism activist, founder of Malu 'Aina Center for Non-Violent Education and Action, arrested numerous times for nonviolent direct action including at the Pohakuloa Training Area on the Big Island. Convicted of federal trespass and related charges across multiple actions. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

expected.body:
Three separately documented 1984 arrests

The original appellate opinion identifies James Vincent Albertini and gives February 4, March 3 and April 7, 1984 as separate Pearl Harbor leafletting arrests. These have separate rows with exact arrest dates. The February count resulted in acquittal in July 1986. The March and April convictions carried suspended prison terms and were reversed on October 15, 1987. Neither suspended punishment nor the reversal establishes actual incarceration or release; those endpoints and durations remain unknown. United States v. Albertini, 830 F.2d 985, original opinion.

Other Hickam and Hilo episodes are not combined with these arrests. Existing identified photograph and the earlier 1972 records are retained. The generic Pohakuloa record still needs independently established custody endpoints.

operations.name: Randy Kehler

expected.name: Randy Kehler
expected.description: Randy Kehler (July 16, 1944 – July 2024) was an American anti-war activist, draft resister, and war tax resister. Working for the War Resisters League in San Francisco from 1967, he returned his draft card to the Selective Service rather than cooperate with the Vietnam-era draft. He represented himself at trial, arguing the war and the draft were themselves unjust, and — refusing even to claim conscientious-objector status as a form of cooperation — was convicted and served twenty-two months of a two-year federal sentence. Daniel Ellsberg later credited hearing Kehler speak in August 1969, as Kehler prepared to go to prison, as a pivotal moment in his own decision to release the Pentagon Papers. From 1977, Kehler and his wife Betsy Corner refused to pay federal income taxes in protest of military spending, redirecting the money to charity; the IRS seized their Colrain, Massachusetts farmhouse in 1989. Arrested for trespassing at the seized home in 1990 and 1991, Kehler was jailed for six months for contempt of court. He went on to serve as national coordinator of the Nuclear Weapons Freeze Campaign (1981–1984) and co-founded the Traprock Peace Center and the Valley Community Land Trust.

expected.description: Ángel Rodríguez Cristóbal was a farmer, Puerto Rican independence and socialist activist who served as a leader of the civil-disobedience campaign against the U.S. Navy's use of the island of Vieques as a bombing range. Arrested on May 19, 1979 along with some twenty others for occupying the Navy's restricted zone in Vieques, he was convicted of trespassing, sentenced to six months in federal prison, and transferred to the Federal Correctional Institution in Tallahassee, Florida. On November 11, 1979 he was found dead in his cell. Prison authorities called it a suicide by hanging, but his body bore a deep wound above the left eyebrow and other injuries, and his family, the independence movement, and much of Puerto Rico believed he had been beaten to death. His death made him a martyr of the Vieques and Puerto Rican independence struggles and set off protests across the island.

expected.name: John Hyde
expected.description: This historical entry was created under the name John Hyde used in The Insurgent. The matching federal court records identify the defendant as John Heid and date his arrest to June 7, 1988, during hearings concerning a women's prison in Washington, D.C. Heid and William Wardlaw were arrested following their removal from the courtroom and a disputed stairwell confrontation with U.S. marshals. Wardlaw was acquitted; Heid was convicted, and the D.C. expected.aka: John Heid (court-record spelling; Hyde is a historical newsletter misidentification)
expected.body:
Court-record identity and exact arrest date

The original appellate opinion, United States v. Heid, 904 F.2d 69, identifies John Heid and William Wardlaw as the defendants in this courtroom incident and dates the arrest to June 7, 1988. Its distinctive hearing, removal, stairwell confrontation and split verdict match the newsletter account used to create this entry. The newsletter's John Hyde spelling and May chronology are therefore corrected in the source record, without creating another profile. The conviction was affirmed June 8, 1990; that decision is not evidence of release. Primary criminal appellate opinion. Wardlaw's later civil appeal independently records the same June 7 event and spelling. Primary Wardlaw civil appellate opinion.

The original Insurgent page 10 was rendered and visually inspected in full. It reports that the judge refused the government's request for immediate imprisonment after conviction. Its requested one-year term must not be treated as an imposed sentence or custody duration. No actual prison admission or discharge date is supplied. Original contemporary report.

The database also contains a later activist profile under John Heid. This is an identity-reconciliation lead, not proof that an existing later-life photograph can automatically be assigned to the 1988 defendant. No photograph is transferred and neither profile is deleted in this correction; their connection remains under research.

expected.description: Katsuki James Otsuka was a Japanese American Nisei from Richmond, Indiana who had been forcibly interned at the Tule Lake War Relocation Center under Executive Order 9066 during World War II. A Quaker and member of the War Resisters League and Peacemakers, he refused to pay 29% of his income tax (the portion he calculated was dedicated to military spending), withholding $4.50, redirecting it to peace organizations. Arrested and taken to U.S. District Court in Indianapolis on August 19, 1949 — alongside fellow Peacemaker Eroseanna Robinson — he was sentenced to 90 days and a $100 fine, which he also refused to pay, resulting in additional jail time. operations.name: Eroseanna Robinson

expected.name: Eroseanna Robinson
expected.description: Eroseanna "Sis" Robinson was a Black Chicago social worker, recreational director, and amateur track athlete who refused to pay federal income taxes for the years 1954–1958 as principled opposition to military spending. A member of Peacemakers and the War Resisters League, she was arrested on January 27, 1960 and charged with contempt of court for refusing to pay taxes and refusing to turn over financial records to the IRS. Convicted in federal court in Chicago before Judge Edwin A. Robson, she was sentenced to one year and one day. She was held first at Cook County Jail and then transferred to Alderson Federal Prison in West Virginia. From her first day of incarceration she engaged in a total hunger strike, refusing all food, and was force-fed throughout. Prison officials released her early after approximately three months, citing the burden on medical staff. Robinson was also a pioneering civil rights activist — in 1959 she remained seated during the national anthem at an outdoor track event at Soldier Field, and in 1961 she was arrested alongside Wally and Juanita Nelson during the Route 40 Freedom Riders restaurant desegregation campaign in Maryland. She died in 1976.

expected.name: Arthur Evans
expected.description: Arthur Evans was a Denver, Colorado Quaker physician and lifelong pacifist who refused all or part of his federal income taxes every year from the early 1940s onward, donating the refused amounts (and sometimes double) to charitable causes. In 1963 he was sentenced to 90 days in Jefferson County Jail in Colorado for contempt of court after refusing to provide financial records to the Internal Revenue Service. He served the full 90-day term. He was one of only six people confirmed imprisoned for war tax resistance in the United States between 1945 and 1965. In a 1962 AP interview he stated: "I won't pay the tax for war voluntarily. This way the responsibility for committing the immoral act is on the government."

operations.name: William Breckenridge

expected.name: William Breckenridge
expected.description: William Breckenridge was one of the thirteen soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment hanged at Camp Travis, near San Antonio, at dawn on 11 December 1917, after the first Houston-riot court-martial (the "Nesbit case"). The executions were carried out in secret, within a day of sentencing and without the War Department review that would normally have allowed an appeal. The Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny) erupted on 23 August 1917 after Houston police, enforcing Jim Crow, beat and arrested soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment. About 150 soldiers marched on the city; the night left some twenty people dead. In the largest court-martial in U.S. history, 118 men were tried, 19 executed, and 63 sentenced to life imprisonment. In 2023 the U.S. Army set aside all 110 convictions and honorably discharged the soldiers. (Recorded as Private William Breckenridge)

expected.description: Eduardo Herrera was a Mexican agricultural worker who had first been held for deportation before being sent to prison. Eduardo Herrera was one of the nine leaders convicted under California's criminal-syndicalism law after the 14 April 1930 raid on the Agricultural Workers Industrial League at El Centro and sentenced to 2 to 28 years. operations.name: Joseph Hofer

expected.name: Joseph Hofer
expected.description:
Joseph Hofer was one of four Hutterite absolutists from the Rockport Colony in South Dakota who, drafted in 1918, refused as a matter of faith to wear the uniform or perform any military service. Court-martialed and sentenced to twenty years hard labor, he was held at Alcatraz — where the men were tortured in "the hole" and hung by their wrists ("high-cuffing") — and transferred to the Fort Leavenworth Disciplinary Barracks on November 19, 1918. He died there on November 29, 1918 after brutal treatment (the Army recorded pneumonia); the Hutterites buried him as a martyr, and his death, with his brother Michael's, became the National Civil Liberties Bureau's "Exhibit A" of the mistreatment of objectors.

Joseph J. Hofer Hutterite communal farmer from the Rockport Colony in South Dakota, drafted in May 1918 along with his brothers Michael and David and his brother-in-law Jacob Wipf. Refusing on Anabaptist grounds to don the military uniform, court-martialed and sentenced to 20 years hard labor at Alcatraz. After four months of solitary confinement on bread and water and "high cuffing" chains, transferred to Fort Leavenworth on Nov 19, 1918, and died ten days later. The Hutterite Church regards him as a martyr.

operations.name: Egbert Aswell Trumble

expected.name: Egbert Aswell Trumble
expected.description: Egbert Aswell Trumble was a Rains County, Texas farmer, an official of the Farmers and Laborers Protective Association, a Socialist Party election official and the Socialist candidate for Rains County sheriff in 1904. He spoke at the first of the anti-draft meetings held in the county in the summer of 1917, called after local farmers complained that their draft quota was unfairly high; at a meeting on July 29 participants allegedly voted that draft-age men should resist induction and that older residents should help them. Rumours that the farmers meant to burn the town of Emory, form armed camps and attack officials proved baseless — no town was attacked, no encampment or arms cache was found, and the defendants did not resist arrest — but about fifty people were seized in raids beginning on the night of August 8, 1917. He was among the forty-six released on individual $2,000 bonds. Tried at Tyler from September 9, 1918 in a trial lasting some ten days, he was one of twenty-three convicted, of federal seditious conspiracy connected to resistance to the Selective Service Act, and sentenced to two years alongside his son John and John O’Rear. The Fifth Circuit affirmed on November 25, 1919, holding that abandoning the planned resistance did not erase criminal responsibility once the conspiracy had formed. He entered USP Atlanta on January 31, 1920 and was paroled on December 4, 1920. His brother Joe and his son John were imprisoned with him.

expected.description: John William Trumble was born on September 24, 1888 at Point in Rains County, Texas, the son of E. A. Trumble, and was a member of the Farmers and Laborers Protective Association identified in contemporary political-prisoner material as a Socialist. At the larger of the two anti-draft meetings held in the county in the summer of 1917 — called after local farmers complained their draft quota was unfairly high — he reportedly led a smaller group away from the main assembly to continue discussing resistance to induction. Rumours that the farmers meant to burn the town of Emory, form armed camps and attack officials proved baseless, but about fifty people were seized in raids beginning on the night of August 8, 1917; he was among the forty-six released on individual $2,000 bonds. Tried at Tyler from September 9, 1918, he was one of twenty-three convicted, of federal seditious conspiracy connected to resistance to the Selective Service Act, and was sentenced to two years alongside his father and John O’Rear. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the convictions on November 25, 1919. He entered USP Atlanta on January 31, 1920 and was paroled on December 4, 1920. He died on May 7, 1952 in Lampasas County, Texas.
