operations.name: Carl Gleeser

expected.name: Carl Gleeser
expected.description: Carl Gleeser was the owner, publisher, editor, printer and distributor of the German-language Kansas City newspaper Missouri Staats-Zeitung, which carried Jacob Frohwerk’s series of editorials opposing American participation in the First World War. The articles argued, among other things, that the United States had entered the war for British and financial interests, that Germany was fighting defensively, and that working-class Americans were being conscripted to protect wealthy investors; the government charged that twelve articles published during 1917 were intended to cause insubordination and disloyalty in the armed forces and to obstruct recruitment and conscription. Gleeser and Frohwerk were arrested together on January 26, 1918 and indicted on thirteen counts on April 23. Gleeser chose a different course from his co-defendant: he pleaded guilty on April 30, 1918, agreed to testify for the government against Frohwerk, drew five years — half of Frohwerk’s eventual ten — and entered the federal penitentiary at Leavenworth the same day as prisoner 12644, so that he was already inside when Frohwerk went to trial that summer. The Supreme Court case that discusses their alleged conspiracy, Frohwerk v. United States, 249 U.S. 204 (1919), was Frohwerk’s appeal; Gleeser never appealed. President Woodrow Wilson commuted Gleeser’s sentence to one year and one day, and when the Justice Department notice reached the Leavenworth warden on May 8, 1919 he was released immediately — after 373 days, slightly longer than the commuted term. He later joined the cooperative colony at New Llano, Louisiana, where he edited the Llano Colonist and helped administer the colony. Born in Germany in August 1855, he died at his New Llano residence late on March 30, 1947 and is buried in the colony’s Gill Cemetery. (Full name: Carl Henry Gleeser)

operations.name: Idell Kennedy

expected.name: Idell Kennedy
expected.description: Idell Kennedy was convicted in the federal wartime speech prosecutions in Washington State and sentenced on June 29, 1918 to eleven years in federal prison and a $5,000 fine — one of the heaviest terms handed down to a woman under the Espionage and Sedition Acts. She remained at liberty while her case was appealed. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the convictions on February 2, 1920 and denied a rehearing on April 5, 1920, after which she entered custody. President Warren G. Harding commuted her sentence effective December 25, 1921, the same Christmas Day clemency that released Eugene Debs and other wartime speech prisoners; she had served approximately nineteen to twenty months of the eleven years. Her prison-admission register has not been located, so the exact date she entered custody, and the institution that held her, remain undocumented. She was tried alongside Frank J. Howenstine, who entered McNeil Island Penitentiary on May 21, 1920 following the same appeal.

operations.name: Mayer Libson Nehring

expected.name: Mayer Libson Nehring
expected.description:
Mayer Libson Nehring was born 1892 in Warsaw, Russia (present-day Poland). Worked as a hatmaker, chiropractor, pharmacist. Immigrated to the United States in 1914.

Anarchist and IWW organizer in Cleveland. In February 1919 he was convicted under the Espionage Act for an antiwar speech and sentenced to nineteen years. At his sentencing the judge declared: “I presume that the Russian Bolshevists would welcome you, and Lenine and Trotzky would be glad to see you back in the event that the government should deport you…in the event that the Government does not send you back to Russia I am going to protect America from your activities by sending you the Atlanta penitentiary for 19 years at hard labor.” His sentence was later commuted on condition of deportation, and he was deported February 26, 1921.

Refused entry at Libau because of anarchism, he coauthored An Open Letter to the Russian Premier Lenin and returned to the U.S., where he apparently ceased radical activity. He received an unconditional presidential pardon in September 1930. In 1935 he applied for US citizenship and was denied, but the decision was reversed on appeal.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
expected.aka: Myer / Meier / Nearing / Mayer L. Nehring

operations.name: Walker C. Smith

expected.name: Walker C. Smith
expected.description:
Walker C. Smith was an IWW propagandist, writer and editor of the Spokane-based Industrial Worker from about February 1912 to July 1913. He wrote extensively on sabotage, direct action, militarism and industrial unionism, including the pamphlets Sabotage: Its History, Philosophy and Function and The Everett Massacre — the contemporary account of the 1916 killings that this database's Everett records draw on.

During the Seattle General Strike of February 6 to 11, 1919, police arrested Smith in a roundup of radicals and IWW members, one report associating the arrest with distributing or possessing a pamphlet on revolutionary Russia. He was among roughly thirty-one people taken into custody in the strike-era crackdown, and was closely associated with the Equity Printing Company, the IWW-connected Seattle print shop that police closed in the post-strike repression. No conviction is documented; the prosecution appears to have ended without trial. Much of his personal life, including his vital dates, remains unestablished.

expected.description: William E. Browder was also known as Will or Bill Browder. William E. Browder was a Kansas City socialist and the business manager of The Workers' World. expected.name: William Hamilton Martin
expected.description: William Hamilton Martin was a National Security Agency cryptologist who defected with his colleague Bernon Mitchell in 1960. The two traveled to Mexico and Cuba before appearing in Moscow in September. At a Soviet press conference they denounced U.S. electronic surveillance of allies and neutral countries and criticized American reconnaissance flights and military incursions. The United States later indicted them for disclosing classified information, but no pending prosecution has been found before their departure. Martin received Soviet citizenship, became dissatisfied with life there, and moved to Mexico in the 1960s.

expected.description: Louis Serafini was one of eleven defendants imprisoned after a September 9, 1917 confrontation at a pro-war gathering in Milwaukee’s Bay View neighborhood. All received twenty-five-year sentences. The trial followed the November police-station bombing, although the defendants were already jailed when that separate crime occurred. On April 2, 1919, the Wisconsin Supreme Court overturned the conviction and ordered discharge from custody in this criminal case. The appellate decision rejected the prosecution’s claimed conspiracy and distinguished the evidence against each defendant. An order ending the criminal case does not establish release from subsequent immigration detention. Sources: Bianchi v. State, 169 Wis. 75 (1919), University of Minnesota Law Library; Dean Strang interview, PBS Wisconsin, “Milwaukee Anarchists, Clarence Darrow, and Justice.”

operations.name: Rudolph J. Vrena

expected.name: Rudolph J. Vrena
expected.description: Rudolph J. Vrena was a drafted man held at Camp Dix, New Jersey, for refusing military orders on international socialist grounds during World War I. Contemporary accounts describe his refusal to sign a soldier’s declaration and assignment card. A court-martial imposed a death sentence, but Brigadier General J. S. Mallory suspended its execution. The Public reported on January 11, 1918 that Vrena remained a prisoner and continued to refuse compliance. That report distinguished suspension from presidential commutation; it does not establish his eventual sentence or release. Mother Earth Bulletin also reported the case in January 1918, using both Vrena and Verna. Later references use Vrana. Sources: The Public, January 11, 1918, pp.56–57; Mother Earth Bulletin, January 1918, “In the Trenches.”
